title: Course-grounded flashcards
scope: Short question-and-answer flashcards covering the core concepts in AM 207 lectures 00–06 and all three uploaded STAT 244 lecture-note sets, with assignment practice and supporting textbook concepts. AM 205 covers PS1–2 and supporting material. No card quota applies; coverage does not imply mastery. Historical and administrative slides are excluded.

cards.title: In binary64, what comes immediately after 99?
cards.answer: 99 + 2⁻⁴⁶. Since 99 is between 2⁶ and 2⁷, the gap is 2⁶ × 2⁻⁵².
cards.takeaway: Machine-number gaps grow with magnitude.

cards.title: Is the machine-number gap the same on both sides of 2?
cards.answer: No. In binary64, the gap below 2 is 2⁻⁵²; above it, 2⁻⁵¹. Crossing a power of two doubles the gap.
cards.takeaway: The grid gets coarser as numbers grow.

cards.title: Is unit roundoff the gap after 1?
cards.answer: No. For binary64 round-to-nearest, the gap is 2⁻⁵² but unit roundoff is 2⁻⁵³: half a gap. Check which quantity a text calls “epsilon.”
cards.takeaway: Nearest rounding loses at most about half a step.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: With three significant binary bits, which numbers fit in [1,2)?
cards.answer: 1, 1.25, 1.5, and 1.75. The two bits after the leading 1 give four equally spaced choices.
cards.takeaway: More bits create a finer grid.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: Why does binary64 round 2⁵³ + 1 back to 2⁵³?
cards.answer: The gap there is 2, so the exact answer is halfway between neighbors. Ties-to-even chooses 2⁵³.
cards.takeaway: Adding one can leave a large machine number unchanged.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: What do subnormal numbers buy us?
cards.answer: A gradual approach to zero instead of an abrupt cutoff. Their absolute gap stays fixed, so relative precision gets worse near zero.
cards.takeaway: Tiny values survive, but with fewer useful relative digits.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: How many binary64 numbers lie in [1.5,2]?
cards.answer: 2⁵¹ + 1. Divide the interval length, 0.5, by the gap, 2⁻⁵², then add one for the extra endpoint.
cards.takeaway: Count gaps, then include both ends.

cards.title: How many grid points a+kδ lie in [a,b]?
cards.answer: ⌊(b−a)/δ⌋ + 1, for integers k≥0 and δ>0. Round down because a point beyond b does not count.
cards.takeaway: A partial gap does not contain another point.

cards.title: Can two different machine numbers have the same computed reciprocal?
cards.answer: Yes. Different exact reciprocals can round to the same output. Rounding squeezes continuous answers onto a finite grid.
cards.takeaway: A one-to-one real operation can lose information on a computer.

cards.title: Does a reciprocal collision proof identify which inputs collide?
cards.answer: No. Counting more inputs than possible outputs proves some collision exists. Finding a specific pair requires more analysis or a search.
cards.takeaway: Existence is not the same as location.

cards.title: Why is 4 × (1/4) exact in binary arithmetic?
cards.answer: Both 4 and 1/4 are powers of two, so they are exactly representable. Their product is exactly 1.
cards.takeaway: Powers of two fit binary arithmetic naturally.

cards.title: Which fractions terminate in binary?
cards.answer: Reduced fractions whose denominators are powers of two. For example, 1/8 terminates; 1/10 does not because its denominator contains a factor of 5.
cards.takeaway: Binary place values are halves, quarters, eighths, and so on.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: Do row operations multiply a matrix on the left or right?
cards.answer: On the left. Column operations multiply on the right: LB changes rows; BC changes columns.
cards.takeaway: Left acts on rows; right acts on columns.

cards.title: Does “scale row 1, then swap rows” equal the reverse order?
cards.answer: Usually not. In the first order, the scaled row moves. In the reverse order, a different original row gets scaled.
cards.takeaway: Matrix operations remember their order.

cards.title: Which right multiplier makes column 1 become column 1 + 3 column 2?
cards.answer: C = [[1,0],[3,1]]. The first column of BC is B times (1,3)ᵀ, giving the required combination.
cards.takeaway: A multiplier’s column gives one output column’s recipe.

cards.title: What does an invertible 2D linear map do to a unit disk?
cards.answer: It produces an ellipse. The map’s singular values are its semiaxis lengths; its left singular vectors give the axis directions.
cards.takeaway: A linear map rotates and stretches space.

cards.title: Singular values are 3 and 1/2. How does area change?
cards.answer: Area is multiplied by 3 × 1/2 = 3/2. A unit disk becomes an ellipse of area 3π/2.
cards.takeaway: Multiply the stretches to get the area scale.

cards.title: What does diag(2,0) do to a unit disk?
cards.answer: It flattens it onto the horizontal segment from −2 to 2. The second direction disappears, so the image has zero area.
cards.takeaway: A zero singular value erases a direction.

cards.title: Why can’t an orthogonal matrix stretch a vector?
cards.answer: QᵀQ=I, so ‖Qx‖²=xᵀQᵀQx=xᵀx. A square Q can rotate or reflect, but preserves lengths.
cards.takeaway: Orthogonal transformations change direction without changing size.

cards.title: Why avoid dividing by a tiny pivot?
cards.answer: It creates huge elimination multipliers. Large intermediate values can magnify rounding errors when later subtracted.
cards.takeaway: A legal division can still be numerically dangerous.

cards.title: Does a zero first pivot mean the matrix is singular?
cards.answer: No. [[0,1],[1,0]] is invertible. Swapping rows makes elimination possible.
cards.takeaway: Sometimes the equations need reordering, not replacing.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review, printed pp. 92–96 · companion practice

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.27, printed p. 93

cards.title: Do elimination multipliers below 1 prevent all growth?
cards.answer: No. Subtracting rows with opposite signs can increase entries. For example, subtract [1,−1] from [1,1] to get [0,2].
cards.takeaway: Small multipliers do not guarantee small intermediate entries.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.27, printed p. 93 · companion practice

cards.title: How do you get det(A) from PA=LU?
cards.answer: Multiply U’s diagonal entries and multiply by (−1) for each row swap. This assumes L has ones on its diagonal.
cards.takeaway: Triangular factors make determinants easy.

cards.title: Why might a flat flag need fewer rank-one pieces than a waving flag?
cards.answer: Repeated stripes create repeated patterns. Folds and shadows introduce extra independent variation.
cards.takeaway: Low approximate rank means a few patterns explain most variation.

cards.title: How is image RMS error related to the Frobenius norm?
cards.answer: For an m×n residual R, RMS=‖R‖F/√(mn). It is the typical error per pixel rather than the total error size.
cards.takeaway: Normalize by pixel count to compare typical errors.

cards.title: Does greedy elimination always improve a low-rank image approximation?
cards.answer: No. Removing the largest residual entry need not reduce total squared error. Truncated SVD, unlike this greedy rule, is optimal for each rank in Frobenius norm.
cards.takeaway: Fixing the worst pixel can worsen others.

cards.title: Why subtract R[:,j]R[i,:]/Rᵢⱼ from a residual?
cards.answer: For a nonzero pivot, this rank-one term exactly matches pivot row i and column j. Both become zero in exact arithmetic.
cards.takeaway: One outer product removes a whole row-and-column pattern.
cards.source: PS2 · Q2 · method comparison · companion practice

cards.title: What if the largest residual entry is zero?
cards.answer: Then every residual entry is zero. Stop: dividing by that pivot would only introduce an error.
cards.takeaway: An exact fit needs no further update.
cards.source: PS2 · Q2 · method comparison · companion practice

cards.title: Why is bx²+cxy+dy²≈1 a linear least-squares model?
cards.answer: The unknowns b,c,d appear linearly. Treat x²,xy,y² as known features.
cards.takeaway: “Linear” refers to the unknown coefficients, not the features.

cards.title: For (x,y)=(2,−3), what is the ellipse-fit design row?
cards.answer: [4,−6,9], because the features are x², xy, and y². The target is 1.
cards.takeaway: The cross-product feature keeps its sign.

cards.title: Does ellipse fitting by equation residual minimize distance to the curve?
cards.answer: No. It minimizes how far bx²+cxy+dy² is from 1, not the shortest geometric distance to the ellipse.
cards.takeaway: An easy-to-compute loss can measure a different kind of error.

cards.title: When does bx²+cxy+dy²=1 form a real, nondegenerate ellipse?
cards.answer: When Q=[[b,c/2],[c/2,d]] is positive definite. Equivalently, b>0 and bd−c²/4>0.
cards.takeaway: The quadratic must curve upward in every direction.

cards.title: Why does cxy put c/2 in each off-diagonal entry of Q?
cards.answer: In xᵀQx, both off-diagonal entries contribute to xy. Two copies of c/2 add up to c.
cards.takeaway: The cross term gets counted twice.

cards.title: Q has eigenvalues 4 and 1/9. What are the axes of xᵀQx=1?
cards.answer: The semiaxis lengths are 1/√4=1/2 and 1/√(1/9)=3.
cards.takeaway: A larger quadratic penalty permits a shorter axis.

cards.title: Why use r=√U to sample uniformly inside a unit disk?
cards.answer: The fraction of area inside radius r is r². Setting r²=U gives r=√U, with an independent uniform angle.
cards.takeaway: Outer rings need more samples because they contain more area.

cards.title: What makes a problem well-posed?
cards.answer: A solution exists, is unique, and changes continuously with the input.
cards.takeaway: You need an answer that exists and behaves sensibly.

cards.title: Can extra arithmetic precision fix every numerical error?
cards.answer: No. It reduces rounding error, but does not fix a wrong model, an inadequate discretization, or inaccurate measurements.
cards.takeaway: More digits cannot repair the wrong problem.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review Q1.50, printed p. 41

cards.title: Why can a smaller finite-difference step make a derivative worse?
cards.answer: Truncation error shrinks with h, but rounding in f(x+h)−f(x) gets amplified by division by h. Eventually rounding wins.
cards.takeaway: A smaller step trades approximation error for arithmetic error.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review Q1.50, printed p. 41 · companion practice

cards.title: Why is subtracting nearly equal approximate numbers risky?
cards.answer: Their true difference is small, but the errors already in the inputs need not be. Those errors can dominate the result.
cards.takeaway: Cancellation exposes errors that large leading digits concealed.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: How can you compute √(1+x)−1 reliably for small positive x?
cards.answer: Use x/(√(1+x)+1). It is algebraically equal but avoids subtracting almost equal numbers.
cards.takeaway: Rewrite the expression before increasing precision.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: How can √(a²+b²) overflow when its answer fits?
cards.answer: The intermediate squares may be too large. With m=max(abs(a),abs(b))>0, compute m√((a/m)²+(b/m)²) instead.
cards.takeaway: Keep intermediate values on a safe scale.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: Why doesn’t x==NaN detect NaN?
cards.answer: NaN compares unequal to everything, including itself. Use an isnan check.
cards.takeaway: “Not a number” follows special comparison rules.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: An estimate is 0.002 instead of 0.001. What is its relative error?
cards.answer: 100%: the absolute error, 0.001, equals the true value’s magnitude.
cards.takeaway: A small absolute error can be a huge relative error.

cards.title: Why is 1.4 a backward-accurate approximation to √2?
cards.answer: It is exactly √1.96. Backward error asks how much the input must change: here, 2 changes by 0.04.
cards.takeaway: Explain the computed answer by a nearby input.

cards.title: If r=b−Ax̂, which right-hand side makes x̂ exact?
cards.answer: b−r, because Ax̂=b−r. The residual measures the needed change in b when A stays fixed.
cards.takeaway: A solve’s residual is a backward-error clue.

cards.title: Can a stable algorithm give an inaccurate answer?
cards.answer: Yes. It solves a nearby problem accurately, but an ill-conditioned problem can turn a tiny input change into a big answer change.
cards.takeaway: Stability cannot remove the problem’s sensitivity.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.64–65, printed p. 95

cards.title: With 12-digit input accuracy and condition number 10⁴, how many digits might survive?
cards.answer: Roughly 8 in a first-order worst-case estimate: 10⁴×10⁻¹²=10⁻⁸. The actual error depends on its direction.
cards.takeaway: Conditioning can consume accurate digits.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.64–65, printed p. 95 · companion practice

cards.title: What does abs(xf′(x)/f(x)) measure?
cards.answer: Local relative sensitivity: the approximate output percentage change per input percentage change. It requires nonzero x and f(x).
cards.takeaway: It compares relative changes, not raw slopes.

cards.title: Does taking a square root amplify small relative errors?
cards.answer: For x>0, it approximately halves them: abs(xf′(x)/f(x))=1/2.
cards.takeaway: Square roots compress relative changes.

cards.title: Can regrouping a floating-point sum change its answer?
cards.answer: Yes. In binary64, (10¹⁶−10¹⁶)+1 gives 1, while 10¹⁶+(−10¹⁶+1) gives 0.
cards.takeaway: An intermediate rounding decision can change the final result.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review Q1.45–49, printed p. 41

cards.title: Why can adding small positive terms first help?
cards.answer: Each might vanish when added alone to a huge sum. Together they can form a contribution large enough to survive rounding.
cards.takeaway: Let small contributions accumulate before mixing scales.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review Q1.45–49, printed p. 41 · companion practice

cards.title: Does printing more digits make an answer more accurate?
cards.answer: No. Precision is how many digits the arithmetic can represent; accuracy is how close the result is to the truth.
cards.takeaway: Displayed digits are not guaranteed knowledge.

cards.title: Can a tiny determinant belong to a well-conditioned matrix?
cards.answer: Yes. For A=10⁻¹⁰I, det(A) is tiny but κ₂(A)=1. All directions shrink equally.
cards.takeaway: Conditioning measures unequal sensitivity, not overall size.

cards.title: For [[1,−2],[3,4]], what are the induced 1- and infinity-norms?
cards.answer: The 1-norm is 6, the largest absolute column sum. The infinity-norm is 7, the largest absolute row sum.
cards.takeaway: Columns for the 1-norm; rows for the infinity-norm.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review · matrix norms · companion practice

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.57, printed p. 94

cards.title: What is κ₂(diag(4,−6,2))?
cards.answer: 6/2=3. Use the largest and smallest absolute diagonal entries.
cards.takeaway: Signs change orientation, not stretch magnitudes.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.57, printed p. 94 · companion practice

cards.title: Why doesn’t a small residual guarantee a small solution error?
cards.answer: The error is −A⁻¹r. A large inverse can amplify a tiny residual.
cards.takeaway: A system can hide large errors along weak directions.

cards.title: A=diag(1,10⁻⁸), b=(1,10⁻⁸). Can x̂=(1,0) look accurate?
cards.answer: Its residual is only (0,10⁻⁸), but the true solution is (1,1). The second component is completely wrong.
cards.takeaway: A weakly measured direction can conceal a large error.

cards.title: Can a real linear system have exactly two solutions?
cards.answer: No. Every point on the line through two distinct solutions is also a solution.
cards.takeaway: Two solutions imply an entire family.

cards.title: If a matrix is singular, must Ax=b have no solution?
cards.answer: No. It may have none or infinitely many, depending on whether b lies in its column space.
cards.takeaway: Singularity concerns uniqueness; consistency concerns existence.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review, printed pp. 92–96 · companion practice

cards.title: Do fewer equations than unknowns guarantee a solution?
cards.answer: No. The equations can conflict. If a solution exists, however, the nontrivial null space makes it nonunique.
cards.takeaway: Too few constraints imply freedom, not consistency.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review, printed pp. 92–96 · companion practice

cards.title: How do partial and complete pivoting differ?
cards.answer: Partial pivoting searches the active column. Complete pivoting searches the remaining submatrix and can swap columns too.
cards.takeaway: Swapping columns also reorders the unknowns.

cards.title: First column: (1,4,−7). Which entry does partial pivoting choose?
cards.answer: (−7), because it has the largest magnitude. The sign is irrelevant to avoiding a small divisor.
cards.takeaway: Choose the largest absolute pivot, not the most positive.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review, printed pp. 92–96 · companion practice

cards.title: Why keep LU factors when solving for many right-hand sides?
cards.answer: Dense factorization costs O(n³). Once it is done, each pair of triangular solves costs O(n²).
cards.takeaway: Pay for the expensive structure once.

cards.title: With PA=LU, how do you solve Ax=b?
cards.answer: Solve Ly=Pb, then Ux=y. Apply the row permutation to b as well as A.
cards.takeaway: Reordering equations also reorders their right-hand sides.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review · repeated systems · companion practice

cards.title: Why can you solve a lower-triangular system from top to bottom?
cards.answer: The first row gives the first unknown. Each later row uses values already found.
cards.takeaway: Triangular structure turns one large problem into small steps.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 exercises · triangular solves · companion practice

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.48, printed p. 94

cards.title: If A=LU, which factor comes first when solving Aᵀx=b?
cards.answer: First solve Uᵀy=b, then Lᵀx=y, because Aᵀ=UᵀLᵀ.
cards.takeaway: Transposing reverses the product order.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.48, printed p. 94 · companion practice

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.44–46, printed p. 94

cards.title: To compute A⁻¹Bc, should you build A⁻¹?
cards.answer: No. Compute v=Bc, then solve Ax=v. This avoids an unnecessary inverse and matrix–matrix product.
cards.takeaway: Apply an inverse by solving, not by constructing it.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.44–46, printed p. 94 · companion practice

cards.title: What does Cholesky need beyond symmetry?
cards.answer: Positive definiteness. A real symmetric positive-definite matrix has A=LLᵀ with positive diagonal entries in L.
cards.takeaway: The quadratic energy must be positive in every nonzero direction.

cards.title: Do positive diagonal entries make a symmetric matrix positive definite?
cards.answer: No. [[1,2],[2,1]] has eigenvalue −1. The direction (1,−1) gives a negative quadratic form.
cards.takeaway: Checking coordinate directions alone misses tilted directions.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review, printed pp. 92–96 · companion practice

cards.title: How do you multiply uvᵀ by x without building a matrix?
cards.answer: Compute the scalar vᵀx, then scale u by it. The work is O(n), rather than O(n²), for length-n vectors.
cards.takeaway: A rank-one map measures one direction and outputs another.

cards.title: Why is uvᵀ rank one when u and v are nonzero?
cards.answer: Every column is a multiple of u, and at least one is nonzero.
cards.takeaway: All output columns share one direction.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review · rank-one matrices · companion practice

cards.title: Why can normal equations make least squares numerically harder?
cards.answer: For full-column-rank X, κ₂(XᵀX)=κ₂(X)². Forming XᵀX magnifies the condition number.
cards.takeaway: Squaring the matrix’s stretch ratios magnifies sensitivity.

cards.title: With X=QR, which system gives the least-squares coefficients?
cards.answer: Rβ=Qᵀy, for reduced QR with full column rank. Project y onto Q’s directions, then solve the triangular system.
cards.takeaway: Separate geometry from the coefficient solve.
cards.source: Heath · §3.3–3.5 · supporting least-squares reading · companion practice

cards.title: What makes X⁺y special among rank-deficient least-squares solutions?
cards.answer: It has the smallest Euclidean coefficient norm. Adding a null-space vector keeps the same fit but increases the norm.
cards.takeaway: The pseudoinverse chooses the shortest coefficient explanation.
cards.source: Heath · §3.3–3.5 · supporting least-squares reading · companion practice

cards.title: Is the binary64 gap at 100 different from the gap at 99?
cards.answer: No. Both lie in [64,128), so both have gap 2⁻⁴⁶.
cards.takeaway: One power-of-two interval shares one spacing.

cards.title: What happens to binary64 spacing when you cross 128?
cards.answer: It doubles from 2⁻⁴⁶ to 2⁻⁴⁵.
cards.takeaway: The exponent increases; the number of significant bits does not.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion concept check

cards.title: Why does nearest rounding involve half a gap?
cards.answer: Any point between neighbors is at most half their distance from the closer neighbor.
cards.takeaway: Rounding chooses the nearer endpoint.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion concept check

cards.title: On the grid 1, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, where does 1.4 round?
cards.answer: To 1.5: it is 0.1 away, versus 0.15 from 1.25.
cards.takeaway: Representable values are a grid, not every decimal.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion concept check

cards.title: Are all integers above 2⁵³ impossible in binary64?
cards.answer: No. In [2⁵³,2⁵⁴), every even integer is representable. The odd integers fall between grid points.
cards.takeaway: Losing consecutive integers does not mean losing all integers.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion concept check

cards.title: Why isn’t decimal 0.1 exact in binary64?
cards.answer: 0.1=1/10, whose reduced denominator includes 5. Its binary expansion repeats and must be rounded.
cards.takeaway: A short decimal need not be a short binary fraction.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion concept check

cards.title: Does a terminating binary expansion guarantee a value fits binary64?
cards.answer: Not by itself. It must also fit the format’s exponent range and precision.
cards.takeaway: An exact expansion can still need too many bits.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: How many points are there in two adjacent grid gaps?
cards.answer: Three: one at each end and one in the middle.
cards.takeaway: Endpoints are like fenceposts, not fence panels.

cards.title: Why can reciprocal rounding lose distinctions between nearby large inputs?
cards.answer: The reciprocal curve gets flatter as inputs grow. Their outputs can differ by less than the output grid spacing.
cards.takeaway: A flat transformation can squeeze differences below resolution.

cards.title: Can 5 × (1/5) still equal 1 on a computer?
cards.answer: Yes. Although 1/5 is rounded, the product may round back to exactly 1.
cards.takeaway: A rounded intermediate does not force a wrong final value.

cards.title: Can deleting a row be written as matrix multiplication?
cards.answer: Yes. Multiply on the left by a rectangular matrix that selects the rows you keep.
cards.takeaway: Matrix operators need not be square.

cards.title: Is replacing row 1 by row 3 reversible?
cards.answer: No. The original row 1 is lost. The corresponding row-operation matrix is singular.
cards.takeaway: Copying is different from swapping.

cards.title: If row operation L₁ happens before L₂, what is the final product?
cards.answer: L₂L₁B. The operator nearest B acts first.
cards.takeaway: Left operations accumulate outward to the left.

cards.title: If column operation C₁ happens before C₂, what is the final product?
cards.answer: BC₁C₂.
cards.takeaway: Right operations accumulate outward to the right.

cards.title: What do the right singular vectors tell you about a linear map?
cards.answer: They are the input directions that become the ellipse’s principal axes after transformation.
cards.takeaway: Right vectors describe input directions; left vectors describe outputs.

cards.title: Why plot transformed disks with equal axis scales?
cards.answer: Unequal plot scales can make a circle look like an ellipse or distort the true stretch ratio.
cards.takeaway: The display can manufacture apparent geometry.

cards.title: Does a negative determinant mean negative area?
cards.answer: No. Absolute determinant gives area scale. A negative sign indicates an orientation reversal.
cards.takeaway: Magnitude measures size; sign measures orientation.

cards.title: Why is an orthogonal matrix easy to invert?
cards.answer: For square Q, QᵀQ=I, so Q⁻¹=Qᵀ.
cards.takeaway: Undo a rotation or reflection by transposing.

cards.title: A pivot is 10⁻¹² and the entry below is 5. What multiplier eliminates it?
cards.answer: 5/10⁻¹²=5×10¹². That huge multiplier is the numerical warning.
cards.takeaway: The pivot is a divisor, so its scale matters.

cards.title: Does pivoting make an ill-conditioned problem well-conditioned?
cards.answer: No. It improves the elimination procedure but does not remove sensitivity in the original problem.
cards.takeaway: A safer algorithm cannot improve the information in the data.

cards.title: What does one row swap do to a determinant?
cards.answer: It flips the sign without changing the magnitude.
cards.takeaway: Swapping reverses orientation.

cards.title: Why is a triangular matrix’s determinant the diagonal product?
cards.answer: Its triangular structure eliminates the competing determinant terms.
cards.takeaway: Only the diagonal route contributes.

cards.title: Can a nearly simple image have full exact rank?
cards.answer: Yes. Tiny noise can make every singular value nonzero, even if only a few are large.
cards.takeaway: Exact rank and useful approximate rank answer different questions.

cards.title: If every image row is a multiple of one row, what is its rank?
cards.answer: One, unless the image is entirely zero.
cards.takeaway: One horizontal pattern plus row weights is enough.

cards.title: If every pixel error doubles, what happens to RMS error?
cards.answer: It doubles. Squaring gives a factor of four, then the square root removes half that power.
cards.takeaway: RMS has the same units as the pixels.

cards.title: What is the squared Frobenius error of a rank-k truncated SVD?
cards.answer: The sum of squares of the discarded singular values: Σ_{i>k} σᵢ².
cards.takeaway: Discarded stretches account for the remaining squared error.

cards.title: A column has m entries and a row has n. What shape is their outer product?
cards.answer: m×n. Every column entry multiplies every row entry.
cards.takeaway: An outer product builds a matrix from two patterns.
cards.source: PS2 · Q2 · method comparison · companion practice

sources.locator: PS2 · Q2 · method comparison · companion concept check

cards.title: Can a sum of k rank-one matrices have rank larger than k?
cards.answer: No. Its column space fits inside the span of at most k column vectors.
cards.takeaway: Each rank-one term adds at most one direction.
cards.source: PS2 · Q2 · method comparison · companion practice

cards.title: How many coefficients does a centered ellipse fit use?
cards.answer: Three: b,c,d for x²,xy,y². “Centered” removes linear x and y terms from this model.
cards.takeaway: Model assumptions determine the number of unknowns.

cards.title: Do three ellipse-fit points guarantee unique coefficients?
cards.answer: No. Their feature rows must also be linearly independent.
cards.takeaway: Three equations can repeat the same constraint.

cards.title: If c=0 in bx²+cxy+dy²=1, how are valid ellipse axes oriented?
cards.answer: Along the coordinate axes, provided b and d are positive.
cards.takeaway: The cross term is what couples the coordinates.

sources.locator: PS2 · Q3 · interpretation · companion concept check

cards.title: If Q has one positive and one negative eigenvalue, is xᵀQx=1 an ellipse?
cards.answer: No. In its eigenbasis, one squared term is subtracted: the curve is a hyperbola.
cards.takeaway: An indefinite quadratic opens in opposing directions.

sources.locator: PS2 · Q3 · interpretation · companion concept check
PS2 · Q3 · interpretation · companion concept check

cards.title: What gives the axis directions of xᵀQx=1 for positive-definite Q?
cards.answer: Q’s orthonormal eigenvectors.
cards.takeaway: Diagonalizing Q uncouples the coordinate directions.

cards.title: For a point uniform in a unit disk, what is P(r≤1/2)?
cards.answer: 1/4, because area scales as radius squared.
cards.takeaway: Half the radius encloses only a quarter of the area.

sources.locator: HW1 · Q4 · transformations · companion concept check

cards.title: What fraction of uniform points in [−1,1]² land inside the unit disk?
cards.answer: π/4: disk area divided by square area.
cards.takeaway: Rejection sampling turns area ratios into acceptance rates.

sources.locator: HW1 · Q4 · transformations · companion concept check

cards.title: Can a well-posed problem be ill-conditioned?
cards.answer: Yes. Its answer can depend continuously but very steeply on the input.
cards.takeaway: Continuous does not mean insensitive.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed p. 39 · companion concept check

cards.title: A perfect solver predicts motion with no air resistance. Why can it miss reality?
cards.answer: The model omits a relevant force. That is modeling error, even if the equations are solved exactly.
cards.takeaway: Computational correctness is not model correctness.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed p. 39 · companion concept check

cards.title: Approximating a curve with straight segments introduces which error?
cards.answer: Discretization error: a continuous object is replaced by a finite approximation.
cards.takeaway: The approximation exists before floating-point rounding begins.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed p. 39 · companion concept check

cards.title: Can higher precision recover digits a sensor never measured?
cards.answer: No. It can preserve available information, not create missing information.
cards.takeaway: Input uncertainty survives a perfect calculation.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed p. 39 · companion concept check
Heath · Ch. 1 review Q1.50, printed p. 41 · companion concept check

cards.title: If derivative error is roughly h+u/h, where is the best scale for h?
cards.answer: Near √u, where the two error terms balance.
cards.takeaway: Do not improve one error source while ignoring the other.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review Q1.50, printed p. 41 · companion practice

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion concept check

cards.title: Can cancellation be harmful even if subtraction itself is exact?
cards.answer: Yes. It can reveal errors already present in the two operands.
cards.takeaway: The dangerous error may enter before the subtraction.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion concept check

cards.title: In a scaled norm calculation, what if max(abs(a),abs(b))=0?
cards.answer: Return zero. Both inputs are zero, so no division is needed.
cards.takeaway: Handle the zero case before dividing by the scale.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion concept check

cards.title: Under IEEE arithmetic, why is 0/0 NaN rather than infinity?
cards.answer: No unique quotient is determined. Any finite number multiplied by zero gives zero.
cards.takeaway: Undefined information is different from an unbounded result.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: Why is relative error awkward when the true answer is zero?
cards.answer: The usual formula divides by the true magnitude. Use absolute error or another meaningful reference scale instead.
cards.takeaway: Choose an error measure with a meaningful denominator.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed p. 39 · companion concept check

cards.title: If √2 is approximated by 1.4, what is the forward error?
cards.takeaway: Forward error measures the answer, not the input.

sources.locator: Heath · §1.2.5, printed p. 12 · companion concept check
Heath · §1.2.5, printed p. 12 · companion concept check

cards.title: Why is the perturbation to b equal to −r when r=b−Ax̂?
cards.answer: Rearrange the definition: Ax̂=b−r.
cards.takeaway: Residual sign conventions matter.

cards.title: Which belongs to the problem: conditioning or stability?
cards.answer: Conditioning. Stability describes how an algorithm handles rounding and perturbations.
cards.takeaway: Separate a sensitive question from a fragile computation.

sources.locator: Heath · §1.2.6, printed p. 13 · companion concept check
Heath · §1.2.6, printed pp. 13–14 · companion concept check

cards.title: Can a function have a large slope but small relative sensitivity?
cards.answer: Yes. For √x near zero, the slope is large but relative condition number is 1/2.
cards.takeaway: Raw units and percentage changes tell different stories.

cards.title: Why can parallel sums differ slightly from serial sums?
cards.answer: They group additions differently. Floating-point rounding makes grouping matter.
cards.takeaway: Different reduction trees can produce different last digits.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review · floating-point properties · companion concept check
Heath · Ch. 1 review Q1.45–49, printed p. 41 · companion concept check

cards.title: What is the idea behind compensated summation?
cards.answer: Track small rounding losses in a correction term so later additions can recover part of them.
cards.takeaway: Do not silently discard every tiny contribution.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review Q1.45–49, printed p. 41 · companion practice

cards.title: Does multiplying an invertible matrix by a nonzero scalar change its condition number?
cards.answer: No, for the same induced norm: ‖αA‖‖(αA)⁻¹‖=‖A‖‖A⁻¹‖.
cards.takeaway: Uniform scaling cancels out of the sensitivity ratio.

cards.title: What does ‖Ax‖≤‖A‖‖x‖ tell you?
cards.answer: The induced matrix norm bounds how much A can amplify a vector’s size.
cards.takeaway: A matrix norm is a worst-direction stretch bound.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review · matrix norms · companion practice

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.57, printed p. 94 · companion concept check

cards.title: What is the smallest possible 2-norm condition number of an invertible matrix?
cards.answer: 1. Its largest singular value cannot be smaller than its smallest.
cards.takeaway: Equal stretch in every direction is best conditioned.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.57, printed p. 94 · companion practice

cards.title: Why normalize a linear-system residual?
cards.answer: Multiplying A and b by a tiny scalar makes the raw residual tiny without improving x̂. Normalization accounts for the problem’s scale.
cards.takeaway: Small needs a reference scale.

sources.locator: Heath · §2.3.5, printed p. 61 · companion concept check

cards.title: If Ax=Ay, where does x−y live?
cards.answer: In the null space, because A(x−y)=0.
cards.takeaway: Nonuniqueness lives in invisible directions.

cards.title: When does an m×n matrix map onto every b in ℝᵐ?
cards.answer: When it has full row rank m.
cards.takeaway: Every output direction must be reachable.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review, printed pp. 92–96 · companion practice

cards.title: Why must complete pivoting track column swaps?
cards.answer: They reorder the variables. Without undoing them, the solution entries can be assigned to the wrong unknowns.
cards.takeaway: A correct value in the wrong position is still wrong.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 2 review, printed p. 93 · companion concept check

cards.title: After dense LU factorization, does doubling n roughly double solve cost?
cards.answer: No. A triangular solve costs O(n²), so doubling n roughly quadruples that work.
cards.takeaway: Reusing factors is cheaper, but not free.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 2 review · repeated systems · companion concept check
Heath · Ch. 2 review · repeated systems · companion concept check

cards.title: Which triangular solve runs backward from the last row?
cards.answer: The upper-triangular solve. The last equation isolates the last unknown.
cards.takeaway: Start where only one unknown remains.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review · repeated systems · companion practice

cards.title: What is LLᵀ for L=[[2,0],[1,1]]?
cards.answer: [[4,2],[2,2]]. This supplies a concrete positive-definite example.
cards.takeaway: A factorization can certify positive definiteness.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 2 review, printed p. 95 · companion concept check

cards.title: Can a positive-definite matrix be badly conditioned?
cards.answer: Yes. diag(1,10⁻¹²) is positive definite but has condition number 10¹².
cards.takeaway: Positive eigenvalues need not have similar magnitudes.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 2 review, printed p. 95 · companion concept check

cards.title: Where must the output of uvᵀx lie?
cards.answer: In span(u), whatever x is.
cards.takeaway: A rank-one map funnels every input into one output direction.

cards.title: If κ₂(X)=10, what is κ₂(XᵀX) for full-column-rank X?
cards.takeaway: Normal equations square the stretch ratio.

cards.title: Which part of y can a least-squares fit in C(X) never match?
cards.answer: Its orthogonal component (I−QQᵀ)y.
cards.takeaway: Least squares cannot fit a direction outside the model space.
cards.source: Heath · §3.3–3.5 · supporting least-squares reading · companion practice

cards.title: Why can inverting a tiny singular value amplify noise?
cards.answer: Its reciprocal is huge, so a small data component becomes a large coefficient component.

cards.answer: It must decide which small singular values count as zero. That decision changes the effective rank.

cards.title: How is a model different from a system?
cards.answer: The system is what you study. A model is a simplified mathematical description of it.
cards.takeaway: A useful model keeps the features relevant to the question.

cards.title: What does a simulation do?
cards.answer: It generates outcomes from a model using specified inputs and rules.
cards.takeaway: Simulation explores the model; observations test its connection to reality.

cards.title: What is uncertainty propagation?
cards.answer: Following uncertain inputs through a model to obtain uncertainty in its outputs.
cards.takeaway: Uncertain inputs produce a distribution of predictions.

cards.title: What does verification check?
cards.answer: Whether the code and numerical method solve the chosen mathematical model correctly.
cards.takeaway: Verification checks the implementation.

cards.title: What does validation check?
cards.answer: Whether a model describes relevant observations well enough for its intended use.
cards.takeaway: A correctly solved model can still describe reality poorly.

cards.title: Why report a predictive distribution instead of only a best prediction?
cards.answer: It expresses which outcomes are plausible and how uncertain the prediction is.
cards.takeaway: Decisions often depend on the tails as well as the center.

cards.title: How does uncertainty differ from error?
cards.answer: Error is a discrepancy from a true or reference value. Uncertainty describes the range of plausible values when knowledge is incomplete.
cards.takeaway: A narrow uncertainty estimate can still miss the truth.

cards.title: What is an event in probability?
cards.answer: A subset of the sample space: all outcomes that satisfy a condition.
cards.takeaway: An event can contain many elementary outcomes.

cards.title: What three rules define a probability measure?
cards.answer: Probabilities are nonnegative, the whole sample space has probability 1, and probabilities add over countably many disjoint events.
cards.takeaway: Disjoint alternatives can be added directly.

cards.title: How do you find the probability that A does not happen?
cards.takeaway: A and its complement exhaust all possibilities.

cards.title: Why subtract P(A∩B) when finding P(A∪B)?
cards.answer: Adding P(A)+P(B) counts the overlap twice. Subtract it once.
cards.takeaway: An outcome in both events is still only one outcome.

cards.title: Why divide by P(B) in P(A given B)?
cards.answer: Conditioning restricts attention to B. Dividing P(A∩B) by P(B) renormalizes that restricted space.
cards.takeaway: Within the new universe B, total probability must be 1.

cards.title: How do mutually exclusive cases Bᵢ help compute P(A)?
cards.answer: If the cases cover the sample space, P(A)=ΣᵢP(A given Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ).
cards.takeaway: Average the conditional chances using the chances of each case.

cards.title: What does independence of A and B mean?
cards.answer: P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). When P(B)>0, knowing B does not change the probability of A.
cards.takeaway: Independence concerns information, not whether events look unrelated.

cards.title: What is an ensemble?
cards.answer: A collection of possible system descriptions or realizations, with probability weights.
cards.takeaway: It represents alternatives, not necessarily particles in one physical system.

cards.title: Do different members of an ensemble interact?
cards.answer: No. They are alternative realizations. Particles within a single realization may interact.
cards.takeaway: Separate possible worlds from components of one world.

cards.title: Can the expected number of molecules be noninteger?
cards.answer: Yes. Every realization has an integer count, but a weighted average of those counts need not be integer.
cards.takeaway: A mean need not be a possible individual outcome.

cards.title: Why is the mean of an event indicator its probability?
cards.answer: The indicator is 1 on the event and 0 otherwise, so its expectation is 1·P(A)+0·P(Aᶜ)=P(A).
cards.takeaway: Counting event occurrences estimates a probability.

cards.title: What is a random variable?
cards.answer: A numerical function of the random outcome.
cards.takeaway: It turns outcomes into quantities you can analyze.

cards.title: Can a probability density exceed 1?
cards.answer: Yes. Probabilities are areas under the density, and the total area must be 1.
cards.takeaway: Height is not probability.

cards.title: What does F(x) tell you?
cards.answer: F(x)=P(X≤x), the probability accumulated up to x.
cards.takeaway: A CDF never decreases and runs from 0 to 1.

cards.title: How do you obtain P(a<X≤b) from a CDF?
cards.answer: Subtract F(a) from F(b).
cards.takeaway: The difference removes probability accumulated before the interval.

cards.title: How is variance related to the first two moments?
cards.answer: Var(X)=E[X²]−E[X]², when these moments are finite.
cards.takeaway: Spread is the second moment after removing the squared center.

cards.title: Is E[g(X)] always equal to g(E[X])?
cards.answer: No. For g(x)=x², their difference is Var(X).
cards.takeaway: Nonlinear transformations and averaging usually do not commute.

cards.title: What makes a stochastic process more than one random variable?
cards.answer: It is a collection of random variables indexed by time or another parameter, with a joint probability structure.
cards.takeaway: Knowing each time's marginal distribution does not specify temporal dependence.

cards.title: If X is normal and Y=eˣ, what values can Y take?
cards.answer: Only positive values. Exponentiation maps the real line to (0,∞).
cards.takeaway: Check the transformed support before writing a density.

cards.title: Why does a lognormal density contain a factor 1/y?
cards.answer: The inverse transformation is x=log y, whose derivative is 1/y. Thus fY(y)=fX(log y)/y for y>0.
cards.takeaway: Density stretches inversely with the coordinate scale.

cards.title: How can inverse-CDF sampling handle a discrete distribution?
cards.answer: Use the smallest x for which F(x)≥U. Each jump of the CDF receives a uniform interval equal to its probability mass.
cards.takeaway: Flat and jumping CDFs need a generalized inverse.

cards.title: What does a PRNG seed control?
cards.answer: It fixes the initial state of a deterministic generator and therefore its subsequent sequence.
cards.takeaway: A seed makes a random-looking computation reproducible.

cards.title: Why must a finite-state PRNG eventually repeat?
cards.answer: After enough steps, a state repeats. Deterministic updates then repeat the same future sequence.
cards.takeaway: A long period matters when drawing many samples.

cards.title: How does a linear congruential generator update its state?
cards.answer: xₙ₊₁=(axₙ+c) mod m.
cards.takeaway: Simple arithmetic can generate long sequences, but parameter choices affect quality.

cards.title: Can passing randomness tests prove that PRNG outputs are independent?
cards.answer: No. Tests can detect certain patterns, but cannot certify every property of a deterministic sequence.
cards.takeaway: Passing a diagnostic is evidence, not a universal guarantee.

cards.title: Why should you avoid resetting the same seed inside a sampling loop?
cards.answer: Each reset restarts the sequence, often producing the same draw repeatedly.
cards.takeaway: Seed once, then let the generator advance.

cards.title: How does uniform sampling on a region D estimate an integral?
cards.answer: Multiply the sample average of f(X) by the volume of D.
cards.takeaway: Uniform density equals one divided by the region's volume.

cards.title: What changes when several x values map to the same y?
cards.answer: Add the density contribution from every inverse branch, each divided by the absolute forward derivative.
cards.takeaway: All routes to the same output contribute probability.

cards.title: For X uniform on (0,1), what is the density of Y=4(X−1/2)²?
cards.answer: fY(y)=1/(2√y) for 0<y<1. The two inverse branches contribute equally.
cards.takeaway: A symmetric fold combines probability from both sides.

cards.title: When does F(X) have a uniform distribution?
cards.answer: When X has a continuous CDF F. Discrete CDFs generally produce discrete probability levels instead.
cards.takeaway: Continuity matters for the probability integral transform.

cards.title: Where must a rejection-sampling envelope dominate the target?
cards.answer: Everywhere the target has positive density, up to sets of zero probability.
cards.takeaway: A missed peak can bias the accepted sample.

cards.title: For normalized p and proposal q with p≤Mq, what fraction of proposals is accepted on average?
cards.takeaway: A loose envelope wastes more proposals.

cards.title: Can a proposal with zero density in part of the target's support work?
cards.answer: No. It can never propose outcomes from that missing region.
cards.takeaway: Coverage of the target support comes before efficiency.

cards.title: How does MCMC reverse the usual stochastic-modeling problem?
cards.answer: Instead of starting with dynamics and finding their distribution, you start with a target distribution and design dynamics that preserve it.
cards.takeaway: The chain is a tool for sampling the target.

cards.title: Is rejection in Metropolis–Hastings an absence of a transition?
cards.answer: No. It is a transition back to the current state, contributing to the kernel's diagonal probability.
cards.takeaway: Staying put is part of the Markov chain.

cards.title: Why can Metropolis–Hastings use an unnormalized target?
cards.answer: The common normalization constant cancels in the target-density ratio.
cards.takeaway: Relative density is enough to decide acceptance.

cards.title: Does an invariant target alone guarantee convergence from any starting point?
cards.answer: No. The chain also needs suitable accessibility and convergence conditions; a chain trapped in one region can preserve the target without exploring it.
cards.takeaway: Preserving a distribution and reaching it are different questions.

cards.title: Does the Markov property make consecutive states independent?
cards.answer: No. The next state can depend strongly on the current state; the earlier past adds no information once the present is known.
cards.takeaway: One-step memory still creates correlation.

cards.title: Why can a very high acceptance rate signal inefficient sampling?
cards.answer: Proposals may be so small that the chain barely moves, producing highly correlated draws.
cards.takeaway: Accepted steps must also cover useful distance.

cards.title: Why can very large proposals slow exploration?
cards.answer: Many proposals land in low-density regions and are rejected, leaving repeated states.
cards.takeaway: Big attempted moves do not guarantee big actual moves.

cards.title: Is one acceptance-rate target optimal for every MCMC problem?
cards.answer: No. Useful rates depend on the proposal, dimension, and target geometry.
cards.takeaway: Judge mixing and effective information, not a single percentage alone.

cards.title: What is the variance of an average of N IID draws with variance σ²?
cards.answer: σ²/N.
cards.takeaway: Independent averaging reduces variance linearly with sample count.

cards.title: What assumption supports the usual 1/√N Monte Carlo error scale?
cards.answer: Finite variance, together with suitable sampling assumptions such as IID draws.
cards.takeaway: Heavy tails can break familiar error estimates.

cards.title: Does a dimension-independent 1/√N rate mean high-dimensional integration is easy?
cards.answer: No. The variance and cost per draw can grow dramatically with dimension.
cards.takeaway: The rate hides a problem-dependent constant.

cards.title: Which expectation equals ∫₀∞cos(2x)e⁻ˣdx?
cards.answer: E[cos(2X)] for X∼Exponential(1). The integral equals 1/5.
cards.takeaway: Recognizing a density turns an integral into a sampling problem.

cards.title: Where must an importance proposal q be positive?
cards.answer: Where the integrand times the target density is nonzero.
cards.takeaway: Weights cannot recover a region you never sample.

cards.title: What determines importance-sampling variance?
cards.answer: The variability of f(X)p(X)/q(X) under draws from q.
cards.takeaway: A good proposal makes weighted contributions similar.

cards.title: What proposal shape minimizes variance for estimating Eₚ[f(X)]?
cards.answer: Under standard integrability conditions, q should be proportional to abs(f)p.
cards.takeaway: Sample where contributions are large, not merely where p is large.

cards.title: Why is the ideal proposal often unavailable in practice?
cards.answer: Its normalizing constant may be the very integral you want to estimate.
cards.takeaway: The theoretical optimum explains the goal without automatically solving the problem.

cards.title: For X∼N(0,σ²I) in d dimensions, where is its typical radius for large d?
cards.answer: Near σ√d, because E[‖X‖²]=dσ² and the squared radius concentrates relatively.
cards.takeaway: Most Gaussian mass is far from its density peak at the origin.

cards.title: How variable is the squared radius of a d-dimensional isotropic normal?
cards.answer: Var(‖X‖²)=2dσ⁴.
cards.takeaway: Relative fluctuations shrink as dimension grows.

cards.title: Why can the highest-density point lie far from most probability mass?
cards.answer: Probability depends on both density and available volume. High-dimensional shells contain enormous volume.
cards.takeaway: Peak density is not the same as a typical location.

cards.title: What is the state of an Ising model?
cards.answer: A configuration of spins, each taking the value +1 or −1.
cards.takeaway: The random object is the whole configuration.

cards.title: For energy −JΣsᵢsⱼ with J>0, which neighbors are favored?
cards.answer: Aligned neighbors have lower energy than opposite neighbors.
cards.takeaway: Positive coupling encourages local agreement.

cards.title: How does temperature affect Boltzmann probabilities?
cards.answer: The weight is exp(−E/(kBT)). Higher temperature reduces the penalty for higher energy.
cards.takeaway: Heat makes energetic differences less decisive.

cards.title: What is the energy change from flipping one Ising spin sᵢ?
cards.answer: ΔE=2JsᵢΣⱼsⱼ, summing over its neighbors with each bond counted once in the energy.
cards.takeaway: Only bonds touching the flipped spin change.

cards.title: What goes wrong if an energy sum counts each neighboring pair twice?
cards.answer: It doubles the interaction energy. Count each bond once or divide that sum by two.
cards.takeaway: Implementation conventions must match the acceptance formula.

cards.title: Why allow uphill energy moves in Metropolis sampling?
cards.answer: They are needed to sample a finite-temperature distribution and can help escape local minima.
cards.takeaway: Sampling a distribution is different from minimizing energy.

cards.title: Where are the minima of (x²−1/2)²?
cards.answer: At x=±1/√2, where the squared quantity is zero.
cards.takeaway: Two separated minima create two attractive regions.

cards.title: Why can a chain appear stable while missing half a target distribution?
cards.answer: It may explore one mode well but rarely cross the low-probability barrier to another.
cards.takeaway: Within-mode stability does not establish global mixing.

cards.title: What units does a transition rate have?
cards.answer: Inverse time. Rate times a small time interval approximates a jump probability.
cards.takeaway: A rate itself can exceed 1.

cards.title: Why evaluate a gain term at n−ν for a jump of size ν?
cards.answer: A trajectory arriving at n after that jump must have started at n−ν.
cards.takeaway: Trace arrivals backward to their source state.

cards.title: Why might mRNA count alone fail to be a Markov state?
cards.answer: Its future production rate can depend on an unobserved promoter state. Include that state to capture the relevant memory.
cards.takeaway: A useful state stores what predicts the next transition.

cards.title: How can promoter switching create bursts of gene expression?
cards.answer: An active interval allows repeated transcription before the promoter switches off.
cards.takeaway: Random switching can create clustered events.

cards.title: What is the state change for one SIR infection?
cards.answer: Susceptible decreases by 1 and infected increases by 1; recovered stays unchanged.
cards.takeaway: A reaction vector records bookkeeping for one event.

cards.title: What is the state change for one SIR recovery?
cards.answer: Infected decreases by 1 and recovered increases by 1.
cards.takeaway: Transitions move people between compartments.

cards.title: Why can a small stochastic outbreak die out even if deterministic dynamics predict growth?
cards.answer: Early recoveries may occur before enough new infections. Discrete chance matters when counts are small.
cards.takeaway: Average growth does not guarantee survival of each realization.

cards.title: Why is a queue's departure rate zero when it is empty?
cards.answer: There is no customer to serve. The boundary must prevent negative queue length.
cards.takeaway: Physical constraints change transition rules at boundaries.

cards.title: When does a basic M/M/1 queue have a stationary queue-length distribution?
cards.answer: When arrival rate λ is smaller than service rate μ. Then P(N=n)=(1−ρ)ρⁿ with ρ=λ/μ.
cards.takeaway: Average service capacity must exceed incoming demand.

cards.title: What remains conserved when two clusters merge without losing material?
cards.answer: Total mass, even though the number of clusters decreases.
cards.takeaway: A changing count can coexist with a conserved weighted sum.

cards.title: What makes a Hawkes process self-exciting?
cards.answer: An event temporarily increases the rate of future events.
cards.takeaway: Past events affect current risk through the intensity.

cards.title: What happens between jumps in a piecewise-deterministic Markov process?
cards.answer: The state follows deterministic dynamics; random events change its evolution.
cards.takeaway: Randomness need not act continuously in time.

cards.title: When can a diffusion approximation miss important behavior?
cards.answer: When discrete boundaries, rare large jumps, or heavy tails matter.
cards.takeaway: Matching typical small fluctuations may miss rare outcomes.

cards.title: What does the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation sum over?
cards.answer: All possible intermediate states, multiplying the two transition probabilities for each route.
cards.takeaway: Break a transition into two time segments and add the routes.

cards.title: What does the generator L do to an observable f?
cards.answer: It gives the instantaneous expected rate of change of f, conditional on the current state.
cards.takeaway: The generator describes local dynamics through test functions.

cards.title: How does the generator determine the evolution of E[f(Xₜ)]?
cards.answer: Under appropriate regularity, dE[f(Xₜ)]/dt=E[Lf(Xₜ)].
cards.takeaway: Local expected changes produce equations for moments.

cards.title: Why does a Markov generator send the constant function 1 to zero?
cards.answer: The value 1 never changes along any trajectory.
cards.takeaway: This is the observable-side counterpart of conserving total probability.

cards.title: How do L and its adjoint L† play different roles?
cards.answer: L evolves observables; L† evolves probability distributions through ∂ₜp=L†p.
cards.takeaway: The same dynamics have a function view and a distribution view.

cards.title: For total jump rate λ, what is the small-time probability of staying put?
cards.answer: 1−λΔt plus higher-order terms.
cards.takeaway: No jump is the usual outcome over a sufficiently short interval.

cards.title: Why does a jump generator contain f(new)−f(current)?
cards.answer: It measures the change caused by each possible jump, weighted by its rate.
cards.takeaway: A generator averages changes, not just destination values.

cards.title: If each of n particles dies at rate γ, what is the total death rate?
cards.answer: γn.
cards.takeaway: Independent opportunities add their rates.

cards.title: How does the mean count evolve under independent death at rate γ?
cards.answer: dm/dt=−γm, so m(t)=m(0)e^(−γt).
cards.takeaway: The expected loss rate is proportional to the expected population.

cards.title: How does the diffusion coefficient scale with random-walk step size h and step time τ?
cards.answer: For symmetric steps ±h every τ, D=h²/(2τ).
cards.takeaway: Spread per unit time determines diffusion strength.

cards.title: How does SSA avoid solving for every state's probability?
cards.answer: It generates individual event trajectories and estimates statistics from repeated runs.
cards.takeaway: Sampling paths trades a huge probability equation for Monte Carlo error.

cards.title: What does “exact” mean for SSA?
cards.answer: It samples the specified continuous-time jump model without a time-discretization approximation.
cards.takeaway: Finite ensembles still have sampling error, and the model can still be imperfect.

cards.title: How do reaction propensities determine the next waiting time?
cards.answer: Sum them to get a₀. With rates constant between jumps, the waiting time is exponential with rate a₀.
cards.takeaway: Any channel can end the wait.

cards.title: How is the next reaction channel chosen?
cards.answer: Choose channel j with probability aⱼ/a₀.
cards.takeaway: A faster channel wins a larger share of the event competition.

cards.title: What happens when the total propensity is zero?
cards.answer: No event can occur under the current time-homogeneous rules; the state is absorbing unless an external change activates a channel.
cards.takeaway: Do not divide by zero or draw a finite waiting time.

cards.title: Why recompute propensities after a reaction?
cards.answer: The event changes molecule counts, which can change the rates of other channels.
cards.takeaway: Each event changes the next competition.

cards.title: What is the count-change vector for 2A+B→3B+C?
cards.answer: In the order A,B,C, it is (−2,+2,+1).
cards.takeaway: Subtract reactants from products, including species on both sides.

cards.title: Why is an A+B reaction propensity proportional to nA·nB?
cards.answer: There are nA choices of A and nB choices of B, giving nA·nB possible pairs.
cards.takeaway: Mass action counts possible reacting combinations.

cards.title: Why does a 2A reaction use nA(nA−1)/2 under a per-pair rate convention?
cards.answer: It counts unordered pairs of distinct A molecules.
cards.takeaway: One molecule cannot react with itself; swapping the same pair adds no new pair.

cards.title: Why can a source reaction ∅→A have constant propensity?
cards.answer: Its supply is modeled as external and independent of the current count of A.
cards.takeaway: The model treats the source as a reservoir.

cards.title: How does a lattice diffusion hopping rate scale with cell width h?
cards.answer: For a neighbor direction, the per-particle rate scales as D/h².
cards.takeaway: Finer spatial resolution requires more frequent hops.

cards.title: Does hopping between cells change total molecule count?
cards.answer: No. One cell loses exactly what the other gains.
cards.takeaway: Transport redistributes material; reactions can create or destroy it.

cards.title: What makes U+2V→3V autocatalytic?
cards.answer: V helps produce another V. The net change is one U lost and one V gained.
cards.takeaway: Existing product promotes further product formation.

cards.title: What is the intuition behind lateral inhibition?
cards.answer: A cell's state suppresses the same fate in neighboring cells, encouraging contrasting local states.
cards.takeaway: Local feedback can produce spatial patterns.

cards.title: How does tau leaping differ from SSA?
cards.answer: It advances a chosen interval and samples multiple reaction counts, approximately holding propensities fixed during that interval.
cards.takeaway: Larger time advances buy speed through approximation.

cards.title: What is the Poisson mean for channel j over a leap of duration τ?
cards.answer: aⱼ(x)τ, using the propensity at the start of the leap.
cards.takeaway: Rate times duration gives an expected event count.

cards.title: Why can naive tau leaping produce negative molecule counts?
cards.answer: Independent sampled reaction counts may consume more molecules than are available.
cards.takeaway: A Poisson count is unbounded, but the reactant supply is not.

cards.title: Why is clipping a negative population to zero not a principled repair?
cards.answer: It changes the simulated transition law and can bias statistics. Reduce the step or use a suitable bounded or exact treatment.
cards.takeaway: Fix the event approximation, not merely its impossible output.

cards.title: What should remain nearly constant during a valid tau leap?
cards.answer: The reaction propensities, with high probability.
cards.takeaway: Small expected change alone can hide large random fluctuations.

cards.title: What does the evidence do in Bayes' rule?
cards.answer: It normalizes prior times likelihood so the posterior integrates to 1.
cards.takeaway: The evidence averages the likelihood over the prior.

cards.title: Is a likelihood automatically a probability density over the parameter?
cards.answer: No. It describes the observed data as a function of the parameter; it need not integrate to 1 over parameter values.
cards.takeaway: A posterior needs a prior and normalization.

cards.title: What is the prior predictive distribution?
cards.answer: The data distribution averaged over the prior parameter distribution.
cards.takeaway: It asks what the model predicts before seeing the current data.

cards.title: Why is fitting calibration data insufficient for validation?
cards.answer: The parameters were selected using those data. Predicting relevant new observations tests transfer beyond the fit.
cards.takeaway: A good fit can conceal overfitting or model mismatch.

cards.title: With a uniform prior and 4 heads in 11 tosses, what is the posterior for the head probability?
cards.answer: Beta(5,8), because the likelihood contributes θ⁴(1−θ)⁷.
cards.takeaway: Add observed heads and tails to the prior's shape parameters.

cards.title: What is the posterior mean for Beta(5,8)?
cards.takeaway: The posterior mean balances the observed counts with the prior.

cards.title: Does the peak of a continuous posterior have positive point probability?
cards.answer: No. A single point has probability zero; intervals have probability obtained by integration.
cards.takeaway: Density height and probability mass are different.

cards.title: Can data restore posterior probability to a region assigned zero prior probability?
cards.answer: Not under ordinary Bayes updating: zero prior times finite likelihood remains zero.
cards.takeaway: A prior's support is a substantive modeling choice.

cards.title: Does a narrow posterior prove that the model is correct?
cards.answer: No. It describes uncertainty conditional on the chosen model and assumptions.
cards.takeaway: Confidence within a model does not establish the model's validity.

cards.title: For N independent exponential observations with sum T, what is the rate log-likelihood?
cards.answer: N logν−νT, apart from parameter-independent terms, for ν>0.
cards.takeaway: The raw data enter through their count and sum.

cards.title: What is the maximum-likelihood exponential rate?
cards.answer: ν̂=N/T=1/(sample mean), assuming T>0.
cards.takeaway: The rate is the reciprocal of the mean waiting time.

cards.title: Is the exponential rate estimate the average of individual reciprocal waiting times?
cards.answer: No. It is the reciprocal of their average.
cards.takeaway: Averaging and taking reciprocals do not commute.

cards.title: Why prefer a raw-data likelihood to fitting histogram heights when a sampling model is available?
cards.answer: Binning discards information and makes the fit depend on bin choices.
cards.takeaway: Use the observation model directly when possible.

cards.title: What is the relative posterior standard deviation for Gamma(N+1,T)?
cards.answer: 1/√(N+1), since its mean is (N+1)/T and its SD is √(N+1)/T.
cards.takeaway: More observations narrow relative uncertainty at a square-root rate.

cards.title: How can a uniform draw produce an exponential waiting time with rate λ?
cards.answer: Use T=−log(U)/λ for U uniform on (0,1). Its survival probability is e^(−λt).
cards.takeaway: Stretch uniform randomness through the inverse CDF.

cards.title: Why does F⁻¹(U) have CDF F when F is continuous and strictly increasing?
cards.answer: P(F⁻¹(U)≤x)=P(U≤F(x))=F(x).
cards.takeaway: Uniform draws choose probability levels, not equally spaced outcomes.

cards.title: How do you turn U∼Uniform(0,1) into Uniform(−2,5)?
cards.answer: Use −2+7U. Scale by the interval length, then shift to its left endpoint.
cards.takeaway: Scale sets width; translation sets location.

cards.title: An event rate is 4 per second. What is the mean waiting time?
cards.answer: 1/4 second. Rate and mean waiting time are reciprocals.
cards.takeaway: Faster events mean shorter waits.

cards.title: You have already waited s for an exponential event. Does the remaining wait depend on s?
cards.answer: No. P(T>s+t given T>s)=e^(−λt), the original survival law.
cards.takeaway: With a constant hazard, the clock does not age.

cards.title: How many more independent samples reduce Monte Carlo SE by a factor of 10?
cards.answer: 100 times as many, assuming finite variance. SE shrinks as 1/√N.
cards.takeaway: Tenfold precision needs a hundredfold sample budget.

cards.title: How do uniform samples on [2,5] estimate ∫₂⁵f(x)dx?
cards.answer: Average f at the sampled points, then multiply by 3, the interval length.
cards.takeaway: A sample average is an expectation; volume turns it into an integral.

cards.title: Does unbiasedness of an average require independent draws?
cards.answer: No. If each term has expectation I, their average does too. Dependence matters for its variance.
cards.takeaway: Expectation is linear even when samples are dependent.
cards.source: HW1 · Q2 · Monte Carlo integration · companion practice

cards.title: Independent values have sample SD 3 across 900 draws. What is the mean’s estimated SE?
cards.takeaway: The average fluctuates less than individual draws.
cards.source: HW1 · Q2 · Monte Carlo integration · companion practice

cards.title: What does MSE include that estimator variance alone does not?
cards.answer: Squared bias: MSE=variance+bias².
cards.takeaway: A stable estimate can still be systematically wrong.
cards.source: HW1 · Q2 · Monte Carlo integration · companion practice

cards.title: Why does a midpoint grid lose its advantage as dimension grows?
cards.answer: With N points in d dimensions, its error scales as N^(−2/d), under suitable smoothness. Monte Carlo’s finite-variance exponent stays −1/2.
cards.takeaway: Grid points must be spread across every coordinate.

cards.title: With at most one million grid points in 8 dimensions, how many fit per axis?
cards.answer: Only 5: 5⁸=390,625, while 6⁸ exceeds one million.
cards.takeaway: A huge total grid can be sparse along each direction.

cards.title: Why can ∫ over [0,1]ᵈ of exp(−Σxᵢ²) factor into one-dimensional integrals?
cards.answer: The integrand is a product of separate coordinate functions, and the domain is a product of intervals.
cards.takeaway: Separable structure can remove a high-dimensional computation.

cards.title: If Monte Carlo error scales as N⁻¹ᐟ², what does 16 times the sample count buy?
cards.answer: About four times smaller error, under the stated scaling.
cards.takeaway: Square-root convergence is slow.

cards.title: Why can symmetric Metropolis–Hastings use an unnormalized target f?
cards.answer: Its acceptance ratio is min(1,f(y)/f(x)). The target’s common normalizing constant cancels.
cards.takeaway: Relative density can be enough to sample.

cards.title: Target ratio is 2, but reverse/forward proposal ratio is 0.2. What is MH acceptance?
cards.takeaway: A proposal’s directional bias must be corrected.

cards.title: How can symmetric MH avoid dividing tiny densities?
cards.answer: Compare log(U) with min(0,log f(y)−log f(x)).
cards.takeaway: Log space avoids underflow without changing the decision.

cards.title: Why is accepted MH probability flow symmetric between x and y?
cards.answer: It equals min(π(x)q(y given x),π(y)q(x given y)). Swapping x and y leaves it unchanged.
cards.takeaway: Acceptance trims both directions to the smaller proposed flow.

cards.title: Should a rejected MH step be saved as another copy of the current state?
cards.answer: Yes. The repeated state records how long the chain stays there. Dropping repeats generally changes the sampled distribution.
cards.takeaway: Waiting is part of the sample path.

cards.title: A chain spends 90% of steps at A. Could keeping only moves suggest 50%?
cards.answer: Yes. A two-state jump sequence alternates A,B regardless of unequal holding times.
cards.takeaway: Discarding repeats discards residence-time information.

cards.title: How do you propose a Cauchy step centered at x with scale γ?
cards.answer: Use x+γtan(π(U−1/2)), with U in (0,1). With fixed γ, the proposal is symmetric.
cards.takeaway: Heavy-tailed steps allow occasional large jumps.

cards.title: What are the Cauchy quartiles for center m and scale γ?
cards.answer: m−γ, m, and m+γ.
cards.takeaway: Scale controls the quartile spread, not a finite variance.

cards.title: Why avoid U=0 or 1 in inverse-Cauchy sampling?
cards.answer: Those quantiles are infinite because tan(±π/2) is unbounded.
cards.takeaway: Finite random-number endpoints need deliberate handling.

cards.title: Does a 50% MH acceptance rate prove good mixing?
cards.answer: No. A chain can accept tiny, redundant moves while exploring a narrow ridge very slowly.
cards.takeaway: Accepted movement is not necessarily useful exploration.

cards.title: For covariance [[1,ρ],[ρ,1]], which directions are long and short when ρ>0?
cards.answer: The (1,1) direction has variance 1+ρ; (1,−1) has variance 1−ρ.
cards.takeaway: Strong positive correlation makes a thin diagonal ridge.

cards.title: Why can both tiny and huge random-walk steps be bad?
cards.answer: Tiny steps accept but crawl. Huge steps usually reject and leave the chain stuck.
cards.takeaway: Tune for exploration, not acceptance alone.

sources.locator: Lecture 03 · adaptive proposal discussion, companion caution

cards.title: Why freeze a tuned MH proposal after warm-up?
cards.answer: A fixed proposal gives a fixed transition kernel. Continued adaptation requires extra validity conditions.
cards.takeaway: Changing the sampler’s rules changes its mathematical justification.
cards.source: Lecture 03 · adaptive proposal discussion, companion caution · companion practice

cards.title: Can a stationary chain fail detailed balance?
cards.answer: Yes. A uniform three-state cycle is stationary but has one-way probability flow.
cards.takeaway: Global balance need not balance every pair.

cards.title: For P=[[0.8,0.2],[0.3,0.7]], what is the stationary distribution?
cards.takeaway: Stationary mass compensates for unequal escape probabilities.
cards.source: HW2 · Q2(b) · companion example · companion practice

cards.title: Why does detailed balance imply stationarity?
cards.answer: Summing matched pairwise flows makes total incoming probability equal each state’s probability.
cards.takeaway: Balanced pairs guarantee balanced totals.
cards.source: HW2 · Q2(b) · companion example · companion practice

cards.title: Does a stationary distribution guarantee convergence to it from any start?
cards.answer: No. A deterministic two-state alternation has a stationary uniform distribution but keeps oscillating from a fixed start.
cards.takeaway: A preserved distribution need not attract every initial state.
cards.source: HW2 · Q2(b) · companion example · companion practice

cards.title: Why can merging Alice and Bob into “not Carol” destroy the Markov property?
cards.answer: If Alice and Bob have different chances of sending to Carol, the hidden identity still matters. History can reveal that identity.
cards.takeaway: A coarse state may forget information needed for prediction.

cards.title: Can two merged states have different internal transitions and still form a Markov coarse state?
cards.answer: Yes, if their total transition probability into each coarse block is the same.
cards.takeaway: Coarse prediction needs block totals, not identical internal behavior.

cards.title: What does whitening do to a Gaussian cloud?
cards.answer: Subtract its mean and multiply by Σ⁻¹ᐟ². The cloud becomes centered with covariance I.
cards.takeaway: Turn a tilted, stretched cloud into a round one.

cards.title: Reaction rates are 2 and 3 per second. What is the mean wait for either event?
cards.takeaway: Competing event rates add.

cards.title: SSA rates are (1,3,6). Which reaction does a uniform draw 0.35 select?
cards.answer: Reaction 2. The cumulative probability cutoffs are 0.1,0.4,1.
cards.takeaway: Select events in proportion to their rates.

cards.title: The next event is at 10.3, but simulation ends at 10. Which state do you report?
cards.answer: The state before that event. Nothing changes before the horizon.
cards.takeaway: Do not let a future event alter an earlier record.

cards.title: What happens when every SSA propensity is zero?
cards.answer: No further event can occur under the current time-homogeneous model. Stop or carry the state to the horizon.
cards.takeaway: No allowed event means an absorbing state.

cards.title: For 2A→B with rate c per unordered pair, what is the propensity at count n?
cards.takeaway: Count actual pairs, not a molecule paired with itself.

cards.title: Why isn’t E[RF] always E[R]E[F]?
cards.answer: E[RF]=E[R]E[F]+Cov(R,F). Correlation contributes an extra term.
cards.takeaway: A nonlinear rate can depend on more than the means.

cards.title: E[R]=10, E[F]=4, Cov(R,F)=−6. What is E[RF]?
cards.takeaway: Negative association lowers the expected product.
cards.source: HW2 · Q3(c) and Q4(a–b) · companion practice

cards.title: With a uniform coin prior, what follows from 4 heads and 7 tails?
cards.answer: A Beta(5,8) posterior: add the counts to the Beta(1,1) prior parameters.
cards.takeaway: Bayesian updating adds evidence to the prior.

cards.title: How does Beta(a,b) update after h heads and t tails?
cards.answer: To Beta(a+h,b+t), for conditionally independent flips sharing one head probability.
cards.takeaway: The prior and likelihood combine through their exponents.
cards.source: Lecture 06 · pp. 45–51 · companion calculation · companion practice

cards.title: With a Beta(5,8) posterior, what is the next head probability?
cards.answer: 5/13, the posterior mean of θ.
cards.takeaway: Prediction averages over remaining parameter uncertainty.
cards.source: Lecture 06 · pp. 45–51 · companion calculation · companion practice

cards.title: Why isn’t likelihood automatically a posterior?
cards.answer: A posterior multiplies likelihood by a prior, then normalizes over the parameter.
cards.takeaway: Reversing a conditional requires Bayes’ rule.
cards.source: Lecture 06 · pp. 45–51 · companion calculation · companion practice

cards.title: Does observing a coin sequence versus just its head count change the posterior shape?
cards.answer: Not under the same shared-θ Bernoulli model and prior. The count likelihood adds a binomial factor independent of θ.
cards.takeaway: Parameter-independent factors cancel in posterior normalization.
cards.source: Lecture 06 · pp. 45–51 · companion calculation · companion practice

cards.title: Can a probability density be greater than 1?
cards.answer: Yes. Uniform(0,0.2) has density 5. Its total area is still 1.
cards.takeaway: Probability is area, not density height.

cards.title: If F(1)=0.2 and F(3)=0.8, what is P(1<X≤3)?
cards.takeaway: Subtract cumulative probabilities to isolate an interval.

cards.title: For density f(x)=cx on [0,2], what is c?
cards.answer: 1/2, since ∫₀²cx dx=2c must equal 1.
cards.takeaway: A density must have total area one.

cards.title: Must you derive the distribution of g(X) to find its mean?
cards.answer: No. Use E[g(X)]=∫g(x)p(x)dx when it exists.
cards.takeaway: Average the function directly over the original distribution.

cards.title: A fair die result is even. What is the chance it exceeds 3?
cards.answer: 2/3. Of the remaining possibilities {2,4,6}, two exceed 3.
