cards.takeaway: Conditioning restricts the possibilities and renormalizes them.
cards.source: Lecture 01 · conditional probability example · companion practice

cards.title: Can two disjoint positive-probability events be independent?
cards.answer: No. Learning one occurred rules out the other.
cards.takeaway: Mutually exclusive is not independent.
cards.source: Lecture 01 · probability rules, companion example · companion practice

cards.title: If Y=2X, why does its density get a factor 1/2?
cards.answer: The transformation doubles interval lengths. Density must halve to preserve probability.
cards.takeaway: Stretch space, thin out density.

cards.title: If Y=−3X, is its density negative?
cards.answer: No. fY(y)=fX(−y/3)/3. Use the absolute inverse derivative.
cards.takeaway: Orientation changes cannot create negative probability.

cards.title: For invertible Y=AX, what is the transformed density?
cards.answer: fY(y)=fX(A⁻¹y)/abs(det(A)).
cards.takeaway: The density compensates for the area or volume stretch.

cards.title: For Y=X², why might one inverse root be insufficient?
cards.answer: Both +√y and −√y map to y. Their probability contributions must be added.
cards.takeaway: A many-to-one map collects mass from every valid branch.

cards.title: If X is uniform on [−1,1], what is P(X²≤y) for 0<y<1?
cards.answer: √y, because X must lie between −√y and √y.
cards.takeaway: Squaring folds both halves of the interval together.

cards.title: Why do accepted rejection-sampling draws follow the target?
cards.answer: Proposal density q times acceptance p/(Mq) equals p/M. Renormalizing leaves p.
cards.takeaway: Acceptance corrects the proposal’s shape.

cards.title: With normalized target p≤5q, what is the rejection sampler’s acceptance rate?
cards.takeaway: A loose envelope wastes proposals.

cards.title: With unnormalized f≤cq, how do you accept a proposal x?
cards.answer: With probability f(x)/(cq(x)). Accepted draws follow f normalized, even if its integral is unknown.
cards.takeaway: You need a valid envelope, not necessarily the normalizing constant.

cards.title: How can samples from q estimate an expectation under p?
cards.answer: Average f(X)p(X)/q(X), provided q covers every contributing region.
cards.takeaway: Weights compensate for sampling from the wrong distribution.

cards.title: p(A)=0.8 but q(A)=0.5. What weight corrects an A draw?
cards.takeaway: Under-sampled outcomes need extra weight.

cards.title: Can importance weights recover a region the proposal never visits?
cards.answer: No. If q is zero where the target integrand contributes, that contribution is missing.
cards.takeaway: Weights cannot repair absent coverage.

cards.title: Why divide a weighted sum by the sum of weights?
cards.answer: It cancels an unknown common scale. The resulting ratio is generally biased at finite sample size, though it can be consistent.
cards.takeaway: Normalization trades an unknown constant for a random denominator.

cards.title: Weights are (1,2,7), values are (0,1,1). What is the normalized weighted mean?
cards.takeaway: Divide by total weight, not sample count.

cards.title: What does one normalized weight of 0.99 tell you?
cards.answer: Nearly the entire estimate comes from one sample. Nominal sample count greatly overstates the diversity of contributions.
cards.takeaway: A thousand draws can effectively behave like one.

cards.title: Why can s/√N underestimate MCMC uncertainty?
cards.answer: Positive dependence adds covariance terms to the average’s variance.
cards.takeaway: Repeated nearby information is worth less than independent information.

cards.title: If integrated autocorrelation multiplies variance by 9, what is the effective size of 9000 draws?
cards.answer: About 1000 for that estimated quantity, under the stationary mixing approximation.
cards.takeaway: Effective size measures information, not stored rows.
cards.source: Lecture 03 · p. 6 and pp. 30–32 · comparison · companion practice

cards.title: In a Poisson process with rate ν, what is the count by time t?
cards.answer: Poisson(νt), with mean νt.
cards.takeaway: Rate times exposure gives the expected count.

cards.title: At 2 events per minute, what is the expected count in 30 seconds?
cards.answer: 1. Convert 30 seconds to half a minute before multiplying.
cards.takeaway: Rates and times must use compatible units.

cards.title: Does independent Poisson increments mean N(1) and N(2) are independent?
cards.answer: No. N(2) includes N(1). Only counts over disjoint intervals are independent.
cards.takeaway: Cumulative totals share their earlier events.

cards.title: If each independent trial succeeds with probability p, what is the mean trial of first success?
cards.answer: 1/p, counting the successful trial.
cards.takeaway: Rare success means a longer expected wait.

cards.title: With success chance 0.2, what is P(first success on trial 3)?
cards.answer: 0.8²×0.2=0.128: two failures, then success.
cards.takeaway: Specify the failures before the first success.

cards.title: With N parents producing two offspring each, why is sibling probability 1/(2N−1)?
cards.answer: After choosing one offspring, exactly one of the other 2N−1 is its sibling.
cards.takeaway: Count the remaining possibilities under the actual reproduction model.

cards.title: With 3 parents and two offspring each, what is the sampled pair’s sibling probability?
cards.takeaway: Large-population approximations need not be exact for small populations.

cards.title: Why scale a geometric waiting time of mean about 2N by 2N?
cards.answer: It keeps the typical wait near one as N grows. The scaled survival probability approaches e⁻ᵗ.
cards.takeaway: Rescaling reveals a nondegenerate limit.

cards.title: Two independent lineages mutate at rate ν for a fixed time t. What is their total count?
cards.answer: Poisson(2νt). Independent Poisson counts add their means.
cards.takeaway: Two lineages provide twice the exposure.

cards.title: Why can a random-time Poisson count have variance larger than its mean?
cards.answer: Exposure-time uncertainty adds extra variance. If K given T is Poisson(2νT), Var(K)=2νE[T]+4ν²Var(T).
cards.takeaway: Random exposure creates overdispersion.

cards.title: How do you invert a linear CDF segment?
cards.answer: Find U’s fraction through the segment’s CDF range, then move that same fraction through its x range.
cards.takeaway: Interpolate in probability space first.

cards.title: A CDF joins (2,0.3) to (5,0.9). Where does U=0.5 map?
cards.answer: To x=3. The probability level is one-third through the segment, so move one-third from 2 to 5.
cards.takeaway: Match fractions along the two axes.

cards.title: Does a flat part of a continuous CDF contain probability mass?
cards.answer: No. The cumulative probability does not increase there.
cards.takeaway: A wide x interval can still have zero chance.

cards.title: How does Box–Muller make two standard normals from two uniforms?
cards.answer: Set R=√(−2log U₁), θ=2πU₂, then return Rcosθ and Rsinθ, using independent uniforms in (0,1).
cards.takeaway: Choose a Gaussian radius and an independent uniform angle.

cards.title: For the Box–Muller radius, what is P(R≤r) when r≥0?
cards.takeaway: The radius is not uniform; its tail decays with squared distance.

cards.title: What distribution does R²/2 have in Box–Muller?
cards.answer: Exponential with rate 1, since R²/2=−log U.
cards.takeaway: A Gaussian squared radius connects directly to an exponential wait.

cards.title: What fraction of uniform square proposals miss the unit disk?
cards.takeaway: Rejection cost follows the area outside the accepted region.

cards.title: How does a uniform disk point become a standard normal pair?
cards.answer: With S=V₁²+V₂² in (0,1), multiply (V₁,V₂) by √(−2log S/S).
cards.takeaway: Keep the angle; replace the radius distribution.

cards.title: If acceptance probability is π/4, how many proposals are needed on average?
cards.answer: 4/π≈1.27 per accepted point.
cards.takeaway: Expected attempts are the reciprocal of success probability.

cards.title: How do you get a two-step transition probability?
cards.answer: Sum products over every intermediate state: (P²)ᵢₖ=ΣⱼPᵢⱼPⱼₖ.
cards.takeaway: Multiply along paths, add across alternatives.

cards.title: With current states in P’s rows, how does a row distribution advance?
cards.answer: p_next=pP. For a column distribution, use Pᵀp.
cards.takeaway: Keep your vector orientation consistent.

cards.title: For P=[[0.8,0.2],[0.3,0.7]], what is the two-step chance A→B?
cards.takeaway: Include both possible intermediate states.

cards.title: What is the basic structure of a master equation?
cards.answer: Probability inflow minus probability outflow for each state.
cards.takeaway: Track probability like fluid moving between containers.

cards.title: Why should all master-equation derivatives sum to zero?
cards.answer: Every transition removes probability from one state and adds the same amount to another.
cards.takeaway: Internal flows cannot create total probability.

cards.title: In pure death with rate γn, how does probability enter state zero?
cards.answer: From state one at rate γp₁. There is no outflow from zero.
cards.takeaway: You cannot lose a particle you do not have.
cards.source: Lecture 04 · radioactive decay, pp. 61–63 · companion practice

cards.title: What does a jump-process generator measure?
cards.answer: The rate-weighted change of a function: Lf(x)=Σⱼaⱼ(x)[f(x+νⱼ)−f(x)].
cards.takeaway: Change per event times events per time gives expected local change.

cards.title: Why must a jump generator send the constant function 1 to zero?
cards.answer: Every jump changes 1 by zero. This is a quick check of probability conservation.
cards.takeaway: A jump cannot change a constant.

cards.title: If each particle dies at rate γ, how does the mean count change?
cards.answer: m′=−γm, so m(t)=m(0)e^(−γt). This mean equation is exact because the drift is linear.
cards.takeaway: Random paths can have a simple deterministic mean.
cards.source: Lecture 04 · radioactive decay mean · companion practice

cards.title: How does a swap increase the left urn’s blue count?
cards.answer: It must choose green from the left and blue from the right. Thus w₊(n)=λ(N−n)(B−n)/N².
cards.takeaway: Multiply the choices that produce the desired change.

cards.title: Why must w₋(0)=0 in the urn model?
cards.answer: The left urn has no blue ball to lose.
cards.takeaway: Rates must respect the state’s physical boundaries.

cards.title: Why does the urn model’s mean equation close exactly?
cards.answer: Its net drift is linear: m′=(λ/N)(B−2m). No unknown higher moment appears.
cards.takeaway: Linear drift lets expectation pass through without approximation.

cards.title: An urn mean starts at 50 and relaxes toward 25 with time constant 25 seconds. What is it after 25 seconds?
cards.takeaway: One time constant removes about 63% of the initial gap.

cards.title: Why is the equilibrium urn count hypergeometric rather than binomial?
cards.answer: The left urn samples N balls without replacement from 2N balls with a fixed total of B blue.
cards.takeaway: Fixed totals make the color draws dependent.

cards.title: With 2 balls per urn and 2 blue total, what are the equilibrium left-blue probabilities?
cards.takeaway: There are more allocations with one blue in each urn.

cards.title: How do birth–death rates determine neighboring stationary probabilities?
cards.answer: πₙ₊₁/πₙ=w₊(n)/w₋(n+1), when the denominator is positive. Normalize the resulting weights.
cards.takeaway: Neighboring flows must balance at equilibrium.

cards.title: Why can a per-jump histogram misrepresent continuous-time occupancy?
cards.answer: Fast-exit states generate many visits but little residence time. Weight by holding times instead.
cards.takeaway: Count time spent, not just arrivals.

cards.title: A path spends 9 seconds at A and 1 at B. What are its time fractions?
cards.answer: 90% and 10%, even if it visited each state once.
cards.takeaway: Equal visits do not imply equal occupancy.
cards.source: HW2 · Q3(e) · simulation diagnostic · companion practice

cards.title: What count change does G+R→2R produce in (G,R,F)?
cards.answer: (−1,+1,0): one grass unit becomes one additional rabbit.
cards.takeaway: Stoichiometry describes the event’s jump, not its frequency.

cards.title: How do reaction channels combine into the expected rabbit-count rate?
cards.answer: Add each rabbit jump times its propensity, then take expectations: (β/N)E[GR]−μE[R]−(γ/N)E[RF].
cards.takeaway: Birth adds; death and predation subtract.

cards.title: What is the rabbit equation in the mean-field grass–rabbit–fox model?
cards.answer: r′=βgr−μr−γrf. It replaces random product moments with products of densities.
cards.takeaway: Growth comes from food; losses come from death and predators.

cards.title: At a positive fox equilibrium, what rabbit density is needed?
cards.answer: r*=δ/γ, because fox growth f(γr−δ) must vanish with f>0.
cards.takeaway: The prey density must balance predator birth and death.

cards.title: Why can a stochastic population go extinct while its mean-field ODE stays positive?
cards.answer: The last individual can disappear in a discrete event. An absorbing zero state can then prevent recovery.
cards.takeaway: A smooth density cannot fully describe losing the last individual.

cards.title: In a coupled Delta–Notch grid, does each cell get its own independent SSA clock step?
cards.answer: Not in the direct global SSA. Choose one event from all cells’ channels using their combined rate.
cards.takeaway: Coupled cells share one global event timeline.

cards.title: Why must the Delta–Notch boundary rule be implemented exactly?
cards.answer: Zero-valued fictitious boundary cells and periodic wrapping produce different neighbor signals.
cards.takeaway: Boundary conditions are part of the model, not a plotting detail.

cards.title: Why set production rate to zero at the maximum count instead of clipping afterward?
cards.answer: It removes the forbidden event from both event selection and total rate. Clipping after selection can distort the timing.
cards.takeaway: Enforce constraints in the event law.

cards.title: What makes tau-leaping approximate?
cards.answer: It holds propensities roughly constant during a time step and samples how many reactions occur.
cards.takeaway: Leap over events only while their rates barely change.

cards.title: With propensity 12 per second and step 0.1 seconds, what reaction count does tau-leaping draw?
cards.answer: Poisson(1.2), with mean and variance 1.2.
cards.takeaway: Rate times step length gives expected event count.

cards.title: What is the MLE of an exponential rate from positive waiting times?
cards.answer: N/Σtᵢ, the reciprocal of the sample mean.
cards.takeaway: More events per observed time imply a higher rate.

cards.title: Waiting times are 0.2, 0.3, and 0.5 seconds. What is the exponential-rate MLE?
cards.answer: 3 events divided by 1 second: 3 per second.
cards.takeaway: Estimate the rate from total count and total exposure.

cards.title: Why prefer raw-data likelihood over fitting an exponential histogram?
cards.answer: The histogram changes with bin edges and widths. Raw-data likelihood avoids that arbitrary binning choice.
cards.takeaway: Binning can change an estimate without changing the data.

cards.title: If θ is uniform on (0,1), are its log-odds uniform too?
cards.answer: No. The transformed density includes a Jacobian and becomes θ(1−θ) in log-odds coordinates.
cards.takeaway: “Uniform” depends on how you parameterize uncertainty.

cards.title: A Gamma(a,b) shape–rate prior meets N exponential waits totaling T. What is the posterior?
cards.answer: Gamma(a+N,b+T).
cards.takeaway: Counts update shape; exposure updates rate.
cards.source: Lecture 06 · Bayesian exponential example, pp. 61–64 · companion practice

cards.title: With prior proportional to 1 for ν>0 and waits totaling T>0, what is the posterior?
cards.answer: Gamma(N+1,T) in shape–rate form. The flat prior is improper, but this posterior is proper.
cards.takeaway: An improper prior requires a separate posterior-normalization check.
cards.source: Lecture 06 · flat-prior exponential example · companion practice

cards.title: What does a 95% Bayesian credible interval mean?
cards.answer: It contains 95% of posterior probability under the chosen prior and likelihood.
cards.takeaway: The probability statement is conditional on the model and observed data.
cards.source: Lecture 06 · pp. 50–53 · transformation companion · companion practice

cards.title: A walk jumps ±Δx, each at rate 1/(2τ). What is its diffusion coefficient?
cards.answer: D=Δx²/(2τ).
cards.takeaway: Spreading depends on squared jump size per unit time.

cards.title: If jump size halves, how must τ change to keep diffusion fixed?
cards.answer: Divide τ by four.
cards.takeaway: Halving length requires quadrupling the event frequency.

cards.title: How does a diffusing particle’s typical displacement grow with time?
cards.answer: As √t: in one dimension, RMS displacement is √(2Dt).
cards.takeaway: Random steps spread more slowly than steady directed motion.

cards.title: What changes between frequentist and Bayesian views of an unknown parameter?
cards.answer: Frequentist inference treats it as fixed; Bayesian inference represents uncertainty about it with a distribution.
cards.takeaway: Both use probability rules, but assign uncertainty differently.

cards.title: What does uᵀv compute?
cards.answer: The sum of coordinate products, Σuᵢvᵢ. Geometrically it equals ‖u‖‖v‖cosθ.
cards.takeaway: The dot product measures alignment.

cards.title: How do you get Euclidean length from a dot product?
cards.takeaway: A vector dotted with itself gives squared length.

cards.title: What is (3,4) dotted with (−1,7)?
cards.takeaway: Multiply matching coordinates, then add.

cards.title: What is the difference between uᵀv and uvᵀ?
cards.answer: For equally sized vectors, the first is a scalar. The second is a matrix of pairwise coordinate products.
cards.takeaway: Inner collapses; outer expands.

cards.title: What is the span of a set of vectors?
cards.answer: Every linear combination of those vectors.
cards.takeaway: Span is everything your ingredients can build.

cards.title: What makes a spanning set a basis?
cards.answer: Its vectors are also linearly independent.
cards.takeaway: A basis spans the space without redundancy.

cards.title: How do you test linear independence using Xc=0?
cards.answer: The columns are independent exactly when c=0 is the only solution.
cards.takeaway: No nontrivial combination cancels out.

cards.title: What does rank(X) count?
cards.answer: The dimension of its column space, equivalently its row space.
cards.takeaway: Rank counts independent directions represented by the matrix.

cards.title: What is the null space of X?
cards.answer: All coefficient vectors v for which Xv=0.
cards.takeaway: These input directions disappear under the map.

cards.title: How do you project y onto a nonzero vector u’s span?
cards.answer: Use u(uᵀy)/(uᵀu).
cards.takeaway: Measure alignment with u, then reconstruct that component.

cards.title: What does XᵀX=I say about X’s columns?
cards.answer: They have unit length and are pairwise perpendicular.
cards.takeaway: The Gram matrix records column lengths and overlaps.

cards.title: If a tall Q has QᵀQ=I, must QQᵀ=I?
cards.answer: No. QQᵀ projects onto Q’s column space, which may be smaller than observation space.
cards.takeaway: A left inverse need not be a two-sided inverse.

cards.title: Why is the split into W and W⊥ components unique?
cards.answer: The difference between two candidate splits would lie in both W and W⊥. Only zero can do that.
cards.takeaway: Perpendicular complementary spaces overlap only at zero.

cards.title: What does positive semidefinite mean for a symmetric A?
cards.answer: vᵀAv≥0 for every v. Positive definite requires strict positivity for every nonzero v.
cards.takeaway: No direction has negative quadratic energy.

cards.title: What does Cholesky express a positive-definite matrix as?
cards.answer: LLᵀ, with L lower triangular and positive diagonal.
cards.takeaway: A positive quadratic can be built from a triangular factor.

cards.title: What is the spectral decomposition of a real symmetric matrix?
cards.answer: A=QΛQᵀ, with orthonormal eigenvectors in Q and eigenvalues in Λ.
cards.takeaway: Rotate to coordinates where the action is diagonal.

cards.title: How do eigenvalues reveal whether a symmetric matrix is positive definite?
cards.answer: All must be positive. Nonnegative eigenvalues give positive semidefiniteness.
cards.takeaway: Check the quadratic energy along each eigen-direction.

cards.title: Why is every covariance matrix positive semidefinite?
cards.answer: vᵀΣv=Var(vᵀY)≥0.
cards.takeaway: Every linear combination must have nonnegative variance.

cards.title: Does rotating by covariance eigenvectors fully whiten data?
cards.answer: It removes covariance between coordinates, but their variances remain the eigenvalues. Whitening also divides by their square roots when positive.
cards.takeaway: Decorrelation removes tilt; whitening also removes unequal scales.

cards.title: What is the compact rank-r SVD?
cards.answer: X=UᵣDᵣVᵣᵀ, retaining the r positive singular values.
cards.takeaway: Rotate input, stretch r directions, rotate output.

cards.title: Which SVD vectors span C(X)?
cards.answer: The left singular vectors corresponding to positive singular values.
cards.takeaway: Left singular vectors describe reachable observation directions.

cards.title: Which SVD vectors span C(Xᵀ)?
cards.answer: The right singular vectors corresponding to positive singular values.
cards.takeaway: Right singular vectors describe visible coefficient directions.

cards.title: How does SVD give the pseudoinverse?
cards.answer: X⁺=VᵣDᵣ⁻¹Uᵣᵀ. Invert only the positive singular values.
cards.takeaway: Undo the stretches that actually exist.

cards.title: What makes the Moore–Penrose inverse unique beyond XGX=X?
cards.answer: It also satisfies GXG=G, and both XG and GX are symmetric.
cards.takeaway: The extra conditions select canonical orthogonal projections.

cards.title: Does n≥p guarantee identifiable regression coefficients?
cards.answer: No. The design columns must also be independent.
cards.takeaway: Enough rows do not guarantee enough distinct information.

cards.title: What is intrinsic aliasing?
cards.answer: Column dependence built into the model specification, such as an intercept plus all group indicators.
cards.takeaway: The redundancy comes from the chosen description.

cards.title: What is extrinsic aliasing?
cards.answer: Column dependence caused by the collected data, such as a group level never being observed.
cards.takeaway: The design can lose information before fitting begins.

cards.title: Why is an unobserved group’s mean not recoverable from its indicator column?
cards.answer: That indicator is all zero, so changing its coefficient changes no observed mean.
cards.takeaway: An absent group contributes no direct information.

cards.title: Why not encode an unordered three-level factor as 1,2,3 in one column?
cards.answer: That imposes an ordered, equally spaced linear effect. Separate contrasts allow unrestricted level differences.
cards.takeaway: Numeric labels can accidentally impose a model.

cards.title: Can a linear model contain x²?
cards.answer: Yes. β₀+β₁x+β₂x² is linear in its unknown coefficients.
cards.takeaway: A curved response can still use linear-model theory.

cards.title: What do polynomial contrasts test for ordered factor levels?
cards.answer: Linear, quadratic, and higher-order patterns across the specified level scores.
cards.takeaway: Trend questions differ from arbitrary pairwise differences.

cards.title: Why does level spacing matter for polynomial contrasts?
cards.answer: The trends depend on the numeric scores assigned to levels. Equal spacing is a modeling choice.
cards.takeaway: Ordering alone does not specify distances.

cards.title: What is the spherical Gaussian linear model?
cards.answer: y∼N(Xβ,σ²I): mean in C(X), common variance, and independent Gaussian errors.
cards.takeaway: The design describes the mean; σ²I describes noise.

cards.title: What is the central mean assumption of a linear model?
cards.answer: The true mean vector belongs to C(X).
cards.takeaway: The model must be able to express the expected signal.

cards.title: For full-column-rank X, what is β̂OLS?
cards.answer: (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. Numerically, solve with QR or SVD rather than explicitly forming the inverse.
cards.takeaway: The formula identifies the estimator; a solver computes it.

cards.title: Why is OLS called linear in the response?
cards.answer: With fixed X, β̂ is a fixed matrix times y.
cards.takeaway: Linearity here concerns y, not the predictor shapes.

cards.title: Under Var(y)=σ²I, what is Var(β̂) for full-rank X?
cards.answer: σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹.
cards.takeaway: Weak design directions create large coefficient uncertainty.

cards.title: Under the correct spherical linear model, what are E[ŷ] and Var(ŷ)?
cards.answer: E[ŷ]=Xβ and Var(ŷ)=σ²H.
cards.takeaway: The fit is unbiased for the mean but still random.

cards.title: Why do OLS and Gaussian maximum likelihood choose the same β?
cards.answer: For fixed positive σ², maximizing likelihood is equivalent to minimizing residual SSE.
cards.takeaway: Gaussian likelihood penalizes squared errors.

cards.title: Can the fitted mean be closer to observed y than the true mean is?
cards.answer: Yes. Least squares picks the closest allowed mean, and can absorb some sample noise.
cards.takeaway: Better training fit does not mean closer to the true signal.

cards.title: With an intercept, how does centered total variation split?
cards.answer: TSS=explained sum of squares+residual SSE.
cards.takeaway: The intercept separates the mean from variation around it.

cards.title: What is R² for OLS with an intercept and nonzero TSS?
cards.answer: 1−SSE/TSS.
cards.takeaway: R² measures the fraction of centered training variation fitted.

cards.title: Why can training R² rise when you add a useless predictor?
cards.answer: The larger space can fit extra noise and cannot increase minimized SSE.
cards.takeaway: Training fit rewards flexibility even without new signal.

cards.title: Does a high R² establish a causal explanation?
cards.answer: No. It summarizes fit, not the assumptions needed for causal inference.
cards.takeaway: Explaining variation is not establishing causation.

cards.title: How is R² related to the correlation between y and ŷ?
cards.answer: For OLS with an intercept and nonconstant fit, R²=Corr(y,ŷ)².
cards.takeaway: Projection geometry connects explained variation to alignment.

cards.title: For known positive-definite V and full-rank X, what is β̂GLS?
cards.answer: (XᵀV⁻¹X)⁻¹XᵀV⁻¹y.
cards.takeaway: Weight by precision before solving for coefficients.

cards.title: What is Var(β̂GLS) when Var(y)=σ²V?
cards.answer: σ²(XᵀV⁻¹X)⁻¹, assuming full column rank.
cards.takeaway: The precision-weighted design determines uncertainty.

cards.title: Why can the GLS hat matrix be idempotent but not symmetric?
cards.answer: It projects using weighted geometry. In ordinary Euclidean geometry, that projection can be oblique.
cards.takeaway: Perpendicularity depends on the chosen inner product.

cards.title: If Y is Gaussian, is AY+b Gaussian?
cards.answer: Yes, possibly degenerate. Its mean is Aμ+b and covariance AΣAᵀ.
cards.takeaway: Linear transformations preserve the Gaussian family.

cards.title: What does (y−μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(y−μ) measure?
cards.answer: Squared distance from the mean after accounting for covariance.
cards.takeaway: A deviation matters relative to its typical direction and scale.

cards.title: For a positive integer n, what is Γ(n)?
cards.takeaway: The Gamma function extends factorial with a one-step shift.

cards.title: What recursion does the Gamma function satisfy?
cards.answer: Γ(x+1)=xΓ(x), for x>0.
cards.takeaway: It extends the factorial recursion to nonintegers.

cards.title: What is the square of a standard normal distributed as?
cards.answer: χ² with one degree of freedom.
cards.takeaway: One independent squared Gaussian contributes one degree of freedom.

cards.title: How do you construct tᵣ from Gaussian and chi-squared variables?
cards.answer: Z/√(W/r), with Z∼N(0,1), W∼χ²ᵣ, and independence.
cards.takeaway: A noisy variance estimate rescales a standard Gaussian.

cards.title: How do two independent chi-squared variables produce an F distribution?
cards.answer: (W/p)/(U/q) has F(p,q) when W∼χ²ₚ and U∼χ²q.
cards.takeaway: Compare independent variance-like quantities after scaling by df.

cards.title: If T∼tᵣ, what is T² distributed as?
cards.answer: F with degrees of freedom (1,r).
cards.takeaway: Squaring a one-dimensional t test gives the matching F test.

cards.title: Is a ratio of any two scaled chi-squared variables F-distributed?
cards.answer: No. The standard construction requires independence.
cards.takeaway: Marginal distributions alone do not determine a ratio’s law.

cards.title: Under a full-rank Gaussian linear model, what distribution does β̂ have?
cards.answer: N(β,σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹).
cards.takeaway: OLS is a linear transformation of Gaussian data.

cards.title: What is the estimated SE of aᵀβ̂?
cards.answer: s√(aᵀ(XᵀX)⁻¹a), for full-rank OLS.
cards.takeaway: A contrast’s uncertainty includes covariance between coefficients.

cards.title: Why is a joint coefficient confidence region generally an ellipsoid?
cards.answer: Some coefficient combinations are measured more precisely than others, as encoded by XᵀX.
cards.takeaway: Uncertainty has direction as well as size.

cards.title: Why scale predictors before interpreting a condition number?
cards.answer: Units alone can create large stretch differences. Scaling helps separate unit choices from near-dependence.
cards.takeaway: Meters versus millimeters should not masquerade as new information.

cards.title: Why use a generalized VIF for a factor?
cards.answer: A factor can occupy several contrast columns. GVIF assesses the block rather than one arbitrary coding column.
cards.takeaway: A multi-direction term needs a multi-direction diagnostic.

cards.title: How should you choose how many PCR components to keep for prediction?
cards.answer: Use an appropriate validation procedure, fitting preprocessing inside training folds.
cards.takeaway: Large variance explained in X is not the final prediction criterion.

cards.title: What can curvature in residuals versus fitted values suggest?
cards.answer: The mean model may be missing a nonlinear pattern.
cards.takeaway: Residual structure is signal the mean model left behind.

cards.title: What can a widening residual funnel suggest?
cards.answer: Nonconstant error variance.
cards.takeaway: The noise scale may depend on the predicted level.

cards.title: Does a pattern-free residual plot prove all model assumptions?
cards.answer: No. It may fail to reveal problems and does not directly check every assumption.
cards.takeaway: Diagnostics provide evidence, not certification.

cards.title: Which plot more directly examines a normal-error assumption?
cards.answer: A suitable residual QQ plot, rather than only residuals versus fitted values.
cards.takeaway: Different diagnostics target different assumptions.

cards.title: What is an observation’s leverage hᵢᵢ?
cards.answer: Its diagonal entry in H. It measures how unusual its predictor position is relative to the design.
cards.takeaway: Leverage concerns x, not an unusual response y.

cards.title: Can changing y alone change leverage?
cards.answer: No. H depends only on X.
cards.takeaway: Predictor geometry determines leverage before responses are observed.

cards.title: What range can an OLS leverage take?
cards.answer: Between 0 and 1.
cards.takeaway: A projector cannot retain more than the entire coordinate direction.

cards.title: What is average leverage for a rank-r design with n rows?
cards.answer: r/n, because Σhᵢᵢ=r.
cards.takeaway: Total fitted dimension is distributed across observations.

cards.title: How does yᵢ affect its own fitted value?
cards.answer: ∂ŷᵢ/∂yᵢ=hᵢᵢ.
cards.takeaway: High leverage gives an observation more pull on its own fit.

cards.title: Under spherical errors, what is Var(e)?
cards.answer: σ²(I−H).
cards.takeaway: Fitting changes both residual variances and their correlations.

cards.title: Why do high-leverage observations have smaller raw residual variance?
cards.answer: Var(eᵢ)=σ²(1−hᵢᵢ). The fit follows them more closely.
cards.takeaway: A small residual need not mean little influence.

cards.title: Are OLS residuals independent just because the original errors are?
cards.answer: Generally not. Their off-diagonal covariances are −σ²hᵢⱼ.
cards.takeaway: Fitting links observations through the shared model.

cards.title: How do you standardize a residual for noise and leverage?
cards.answer: rᵢ=eᵢ/[s√(1−hᵢᵢ)], when the denominator is positive.
cards.takeaway: Raw residuals do not all have the same variance.

cards.title: Why isn’t an internally studentized residual exactly t-distributed?
cards.answer: Its numerator and the full-data estimate s are dependent.
cards.takeaway: The usual t construction needs an independent noise estimate.

cards.title: What changes for an externally studentized residual?
cards.answer: Use s estimated with observation i omitted: eᵢ/[s₍ᵢ₎√(1−hᵢᵢ)].
cards.takeaway: Estimate noise without the point being checked.

cards.title: Under Gaussian errors, what is the deleted-residual t reference?
cards.answer: t with n−p−1 df for a fixed observation, assuming the deleted design keeps rank p.
cards.takeaway: Deleting one observation costs one residual degree of freedom.

cards.title: Why adjust when testing every observation for outlyingness?
cards.answer: Many individual tests increase the chance of at least one false flag.
cards.takeaway: Searching everywhere is different from checking one prespecified point.

cards.title: How does Bonferroni adjust n residual-test p-values?
cards.answer: Multiply each raw p-value by n and cap at 1.
cards.takeaway: Spend the error budget across the whole search.

cards.title: Does Bonferroni require independent residual tests?
cards.answer: No. Its familywise-error bound also holds under dependence.
cards.takeaway: The union bound does not need independence.

cards.title: Which reference quantiles match externally studentized residuals under the Gaussian model?
cards.answer: t quantiles with n−p−1 df, subject to the deletion assumptions.
cards.takeaway: Use the distribution of the actual diagnostic you plotted.

cards.title: What happens to XᵀX when observation i is removed?
cards.answer: Subtract xᵢᵀxᵢ.
cards.takeaway: One deleted row is a rank-one update to the Gram matrix.

cards.title: Why is Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury useful for deletion diagnostics?
cards.answer: It updates an inverse after a low-rank change instead of recomputing it from scratch, when the needed inverses exist.
cards.takeaway: Reuse the full fit to study many nearby fits.

cards.title: How is the leave-one-out prediction residual related to the full-fit residual?
cards.answer: It is eᵢ/(1−hᵢᵢ), provided deleting the point preserves rank.
cards.takeaway: The full fit hides some error by fitting the point itself.

cards.title: Why can deleting a high-leverage point cause a large change?
cards.answer: Deletion formulas divide by 1−hᵢᵢ, which becomes small.
cards.takeaway: A point with strong pull can be hard to replace.

cards.title: What warning does hᵢᵢ=1 give for ordinary deletion formulas?
cards.answer: The denominator vanishes; deleting that observation loses a design direction.
cards.takeaway: Some observations uniquely support part of the model.

cards.title: How do outlyingness and leverage differ?
cards.answer: Outlyingness is an unusual response given x; leverage is an unusual x.
cards.takeaway: A point can be unusual in either axis of the modeling problem.

cards.title: What does influence ask?
cards.answer: How much the fitted model changes when an observation is removed.
cards.takeaway: Influence is about the fit’s dependence on a point.

cards.title: Must a high-leverage point be highly influential?
cards.answer: No. Its response may agree closely with the rest of the fitted pattern.
cards.takeaway: Potential pull is different from actual disruption.

cards.title: What does Cook’s distance summarize?
cards.answer: The coefficient change after deleting a point, scaled by coefficient uncertainty and model dimension.
cards.takeaway: Compare deletion effects on a common uncertainty scale.

cards.title: How does Cook’s distance combine residual size and leverage?
cards.answer: Dᵢ=(rᵢ²/p)hᵢᵢ/(1−hᵢᵢ), using the internally studentized residual.
cards.takeaway: Large residuals and high leverage reinforce each other.

cards.title: Does a large Cook’s distance automatically justify deleting an observation?
cards.answer: No. Investigate data quality and model sensitivity; the point may be valid and important.
cards.takeaway: A diagnostic flag starts an investigation, not an automatic deletion.

cards.title: What distinguishes DFFITS from DFBETAS?
cards.answer: DFFITS focuses on a fitted-value change; DFBETAS on a particular coefficient change.
cards.takeaway: Different influence measures target different consequences.

cards.title: What does the column space of X mean in regression?
cards.answer: It is every mean vector the model can express: all Xβ. It contains zero and is closed under addition and scaling.
cards.takeaway: The column space is the model’s menu of possible means.

cards.title: For an n×p design X, do coefficients and fitted values live in the same space?
cards.answer: Usually not. β lives in ℝᵖ; Xβ lives in ℝⁿ.
cards.takeaway: Coefficients describe features; fitted values describe observations.

sources.locator: Linear algebra notes · subspaces and rank

cards.title: A 10×4 design has rank 3. How many coefficient directions are invisible?
cards.answer: One: dim N(X)=4−3. Moving along it leaves Xβ unchanged.
cards.takeaway: Rank counts visible directions; nullity counts invisible ones.
cards.source: Linear algebra notes · subspaces and rank · companion practice

cards.title: Can different design matrices describe the same mean model?
cards.answer: Yes, if their columns span the same space.
cards.takeaway: The reachable means matter more than the chosen basis.

cards.title: What vectors are perpendicular to (1,1,0) and (0,1,1)?
cards.answer: Multiples of (1,−1,1). Each dot product is zero.
cards.takeaway: Perpendicular directions satisfy all column constraints at once.

cards.title: Why is N(X) perpendicular to the row space of X?
cards.answer: Xv=0 says every row has dot product zero with v. The same is then true for every combination of rows.
cards.takeaway: A null direction is invisible to every row.

cards.title: Project y=(1,2,6) onto the constant vectors. What do you get?
cards.answer: (3,3,3), using the average 3. The residual is (−2,−1,3).
cards.takeaway: The best constant fit is the average.

cards.title: When can ℓᵀβ be estimated linearly and without bias?
cards.answer: When ℓ is in X’s row space. Then ℓ=Xᵀa for some a, and aᵀy estimates the target unbiasedly.
cards.takeaway: An estimable target cannot depend on invisible coefficient directions.

cards.title: With X=[x x], which is identifiable: β₁ or β₁+β₂?
cards.answer: The sum. The mean is x(β₁+β₂), so the data cannot separate the two contributions.
cards.takeaway: Duplicate features reveal a total, not its allocation.

cards.title: If ℓ=Xᵀa, why is aᵀy unbiased for ℓᵀβ?
cards.answer: E[aᵀy]=aᵀXβ=ℓᵀβ, assuming E[y]=Xβ.
cards.takeaway: Match the estimator’s mean to the target.

cards.title: Can γ₂−γ₁ be identifiable when individual group effects are not?
cards.answer: Yes. In μᵢ=α+γᵢ, the difference is μ₂−μ₁ for observed groups. A common shift in effects cancels.
cards.takeaway: Differences can be identifiable even when baselines are arbitrary.

cards.title: With rank-deficient X, when is a new mean x₀β uniquely determined?
cards.answer: When x₀ is in X’s row space. Otherwise two equally valid coefficient vectors can predict different new means.
cards.takeaway: Training-fit agreement does not guarantee prediction agreement everywhere.

cards.title: Does a numerically accurate least-squares fit guarantee valid inference?
cards.answer: No. AM 205 asks whether the calculation is reliable; STAT 244 asks whether the statistical assumptions justify inference.
cards.takeaway: Accurate computation does not validate the model’s assumptions.

cards.title: Why can an intercept plus every group indicator cause ambiguity?
cards.answer: The indicators add up to the intercept column. You can shift the intercept and offset every group effect without changing the fit.
cards.takeaway: Redundant columns create redundant coefficient descriptions.

cards.title: An intercept plus three observed-group indicators gives how many independent directions?
cards.answer: Three, not four. The intercept is the sum of the indicators.
cards.takeaway: Count independent directions, not column names.

cards.title: Does choosing a reference group restrict the possible group means?
cards.answer: No. It changes the coefficient description: the intercept is the reference mean, and other effects are differences.
cards.takeaway: An identifying convention is not a substantive hypothesis.

cards.title: Why do X and XA give the same fits when A is invertible?
cards.answer: They span the same column space. A changes coordinates, not the set of possible mean vectors.
cards.takeaway: Recode the coefficients without changing the model.

cards.title: If X*=XA and X has full column rank, how do coefficients transform?
cards.answer: β=Aγ, or γ=A⁻¹β, so Xβ=X*γ.
cards.takeaway: The coefficients must compensate for the changed basis.
cards.source: HW2 · Q1 and Q4 · companion practice

cards.title: Two full-rank designs share a column space. Can the basis-change matrix be singular?
cards.answer: No. A singular change would lose a direction, contradicting full column rank.
cards.takeaway: A genuine basis change preserves every direction.
cards.source: HW2 · Q1 and Q4 · companion practice

cards.title: If β̂ is one least-squares solution, what are all the others?
cards.answer: β̂+N(X). Adding a null vector changes coefficients but leaves the fitted values unchanged.
cards.takeaway: Nonunique solutions form a shifted null space.

cards.title: If X=[x x] and the best fit is 3x, what coefficient pairs work?
cards.answer: Every pair with β₁+β₂=3, such as (3,0) or (1,2).
cards.takeaway: One fit can have many coefficient explanations.

cards.title: Do the normal equations require normally distributed errors?
cards.answer: No. “Normal” means perpendicular: Xᵀ(y−Xβ̂)=0. This follows from least-squares geometry alone.
cards.takeaway: The name refers to a right angle, not a distribution.

cards.title: What is the gradient of ‖y−Xβ‖²?
cards.answer: 2Xᵀ(Xβ−y). Setting it to zero gives XᵀXβ=Xᵀy.
cards.takeaway: At the optimum, no predictor direction reduces squared error.

cards.title: Why do OLS residuals sum to zero when there is an intercept?
cards.answer: They are perpendicular to every design column, including the all-ones column. So 1ᵀe=0.
cards.takeaway: An intercept forces the average residual to zero.

cards.title: Why are OLS fitted values perpendicular to residuals?
cards.answer: The fit lies in C(X), and the residual is perpendicular to that entire space.
cards.takeaway: Least squares splits data into a fit and an orthogonal leftover.

cards.title: Which two properties define an orthogonal projector P?
cards.answer: P²=P and Pᵀ=P. Applying it twice changes nothing, and symmetry makes the projection perpendicular.
cards.takeaway: Idempotence gives a projection; symmetry makes it orthogonal.

cards.title: Is P²=P alone enough for an orthogonal projection?
cards.answer: No. [[1,1],[0,0]] is idempotent but not symmetric. It projects at a slant.
cards.takeaway: A projection can be oblique.

cards.title: What eigenvalues can a projector have?
cards.answer: Only 0 or 1: λ²=λ. A direction is either removed or retained.
cards.takeaway: A projector selects directions rather than stretching them.

cards.title: If the model space has rank r, what is tr(H)?
cards.answer: r. Each retained direction contributes an eigenvalue 1.
cards.takeaway: The hat matrix’s trace counts fitted dimensions.

cards.title: For nested models, what does (P₁−P₀)y represent?
cards.answer: The part of y explained by the larger model but not the smaller one.
cards.takeaway: Added directions account for the improvement in fit.

cards.title: If V₀⊆V₁, why is P₁P₀=P₀?
cards.answer: After projecting into V₀, the vector already lies in V₁. Projecting into V₁ cannot change it.
cards.takeaway: A larger space already contains the smaller fit.

cards.title: Is the difference of two orthogonal projectors always a projector?
cards.answer: No. diag(0,1)−diag(1,0)=diag(−1,1), which is not idempotent. The usual difference rule requires nested spaces.
cards.takeaway: Subtracting unrelated model spaces is not “extra fit.”

cards.title: Under treatment coding, what does the intercept mean?
cards.answer: The fitted reference-group mean when other numeric predictors are zero.
cards.takeaway: The coding determines the baseline’s interpretation.

cards.title: Reference mean 10; B’s coefficient is 2. What is B’s fitted mean?
cards.answer: 12. Treatment coefficients are differences from the reference.
cards.takeaway: Add the contrast to the baseline.

cards.title: Sum-coded effects are 2 and −1 for three groups. What is the missing effect?
cards.answer: −1, so all three effects sum to zero.
cards.takeaway: The final effect is determined by the constraint.

cards.title: With a contrast coded −1 for A and +1 for B, why is its coefficient half their difference?
cards.answer: Moving from A to B changes the code by 2, so the fitted difference is twice the coefficient.
cards.takeaway: Read the coding scale before interpreting a coefficient.

cards.title: Can you drop the intercept from any equivalent factor codings and keep equivalent models?
cards.answer: No. Their spaces can coincide only after the intercept direction is added.
cards.takeaway: Removing a shared direction can reveal different remaining spaces.

cards.title: Why divide residual SSE by n−rank(X) to estimate noise variance unbiasedly?
cards.answer: Fitting uses rank(X) directions. Under spherical errors and the correct mean model, only n−rank(X) noise directions remain in the residual.
cards.takeaway: Fitted directions consume residual degrees of freedom.

cards.title: n=20, rank(X)=4, SSE=80. What is the unbiased variance estimate?
cards.takeaway: Divide by residual dimensions, not total observations.
cards.source: HW2 · Q7; least-squares theory · companion practice

cards.title: Why is SSE/n a likelihood maximum for Gaussian variance when SSE>0?
cards.answer: At s=SSE/n, the derivative of ℓ(s) is zero and its second derivative is negative.
cards.takeaway: Check curvature, not just the stationary point.
cards.source: HW2 · Q7; least-squares theory · companion practice

cards.title: What does “best” mean in BLUE?
cards.answer: Smallest variance among linear unbiased estimators, under the Gauss–Markov assumptions. It does not compare against every biased or nonlinear estimator.
cards.takeaway: “Best” always has a comparison class.

cards.title: Does OLS need Gaussian errors to be unbiased?
cards.answer: No. With fixed full-rank X, E[y]=Xβ is enough. Gaussianity matters for exact finite-sample t and F inference.
cards.takeaway: Estimation and exact inference require different assumptions.

cards.title: What identity defines a generalized inverse G of B here?
cards.answer: BGB=B. It need not satisfy BG=I or be unique.
cards.takeaway: A generalized inverse only has to undo B where B acts.

cards.title: For B=diag(1,0), why does G=diag(1,t) work for any t?
cards.answer: BGB=B whatever t is. Multiplication by B erases the second direction.
cards.takeaway: The generalized-inverse rule leaves invisible directions unconstrained.
cards.source: Linear algebra notes · pp. 4–5 · companion practice

cards.title: If G is a generalized inverse of B, what works for BA when A is invertible?
cards.answer: A⁻¹G, since (BA)(A⁻¹G)(BA)=BGBA=BA.
cards.takeaway: Cancel A next to its inverse, then use BGB=B.

cards.title: If G is a generalized inverse of B, what works for AB when A is invertible?
cards.answer: GA⁻¹, since (AB)(GA⁻¹)(AB)=A(BGB)=AB.
cards.takeaway: The inverse must go on the correct side.

cards.title: Why can coefficients be nonunique while fitted values are unique?
cards.answer: All least-squares fits equal the unique orthogonal projection onto C(X). Different coefficient solutions differ only in N(X).
cards.takeaway: The prediction vector is unique even if its coordinates are not.

cards.title: For X=[[1,0],[1,0]] and y=(1,3), what is the fit?
cards.answer: (2,2). The first coefficient is 2; the second is arbitrary because its column is zero.
cards.takeaway: An unused coefficient cannot affect predictions.

cards.title: Why is an orthogonal projection the nearest point in a subspace?
cards.answer: Moving elsewhere within the subspace adds a perpendicular squared-distance term: ‖y−μ‖²=‖y−μ̂‖²+‖μ̂−μ‖².
cards.takeaway: Every alternative adds nonnegative extra distance.

cards.title: Why can a linear unbiased competitor not beat OLS under spherical errors?
cards.answer: Its covariance is OLS covariance plus σ²AAᵀ for some AX=0. The added term is positive semidefinite.
cards.takeaway: Extra unbiased adjustments add noise, not information.

cards.title: A linear unbiased contrast estimator adds weights z with Xᵀz=0. What variance does that add?
cards.answer: σ²‖z‖² under Var(y)=σ²I.
cards.takeaway: Weighting pure residual directions adds noise to the target.

cards.title: What does generalized least squares change?
cards.answer: It measures residual size using V⁻¹ when Var(y)=σ²V: minimize eᵀV⁻¹e.
cards.takeaway: Judge errors relative to their covariance structure.

cards.title: Why whiten both y and X in GLS?
cards.answer: Transforming y by V⁻¹ᐟ² changes its mean to V⁻¹ᐟ²Xβ too. Leaving X unchanged would change the model.
cards.takeaway: Transform the data and its expected signal together.

cards.title: Two independent measurements have variances 1 and 4. What relative weights should they get?
cards.answer: 1 and 1/4, proportional to inverse variance.
cards.takeaway: Trust the noisier measurement less.

cards.title: Values are 2 and 8, with variances proportional to 1 and 4. What is their weighted mean?
cards.takeaway: The estimate leans toward the more precise observation.

cards.title: Project a standard Gaussian vector onto r orthogonal directions. What distribution does its squared length have?
cards.answer: χ² with r degrees of freedom: a sum of r independent squared standard normals.
cards.takeaway: Degrees of freedom count independent squared noise directions.

cards.title: What are the mean and variance of Z₁²+Z₂² for independent standard normals?
cards.answer: It is χ²₂, with mean 2 and variance 4.
cards.takeaway: For χ²ᵣ, mean is r and variance is 2r.

cards.title: Why are Gaussian OLS fitted values and residuals independent?
cards.answer: They are jointly Gaussian and have zero cross-covariance, since H(I−H)=0.
cards.takeaway: Gaussianity turns orthogonality into independence.

cards.title: What does the nested-model F statistic compare?
cards.answer: Improvement per added direction against residual noise per remaining direction: [(SSE₀−SSE₁)/(r₁−r₀)]/[SSE₁/(n−r₁)].
cards.takeaway: Ask whether extra fit is large relative to noise.

cards.title: Why is the usual central F reference distribution a null-model result?
cards.answer: Under the null, the extra fitted directions contain noise but no mean signal. Under an alternative, they can contain signal too.
cards.takeaway: A test’s reference describes what happens without the added effect.

cards.title: How many test degrees of freedom can a four-level factor add?
cards.answer: Three with an intercept, if all three contrast directions are independent.
cards.takeaway: One named predictor can contribute several directions.

cards.title: For nested Gaussian models, do a large F statistic and a small null/full likelihood ratio agree?
cards.answer: Yes. Both indicate that allowing the extra directions substantially improves fit.
cards.takeaway: Different statistics can encode the same evidence ordering.

cards.title: SSE drops from 120 to 80 after adding 2 directions; full residual df is 20. What is F?
cards.takeaway: Compare improvement per direction with noise per direction.

cards.title: How do you express β₂=β₃ as a linear restriction?
cards.answer: Use a row with 1 in position 2, −1 in position 3, and zeros elsewhere; set its product with β to zero.
cards.takeaway: Equality is a zero difference.

cards.title: Is the restriction β₃=2 a subspace constraint?
cards.answer: No. Its solution set does not contain zero, so it is affine.
cards.takeaway: A nonzero target shifts the constraint away from the origin.

cards.title: Why add Lagrange multipliers to constrained least squares?
cards.answer: They balance the least-squares gradient against directions forbidden by Λβ=c. The constraints and stationarity equations are solved together.
cards.takeaway: The best allowed point need not have an unconstrained zero gradient.

cards.title: What is a coefficient’s estimated standard error in full-rank OLS?
cards.answer: s√[(XᵀX)⁻¹ⱼⱼ], with s²=SSE/(n−p). The inverse-design term alone omits the noise scale.
cards.takeaway: Uncertainty combines design geometry and noise size.

cards.title: If s=3 and (XᵀX)⁻¹ⱼⱼ=0.04, what is the coefficient SE?
cards.takeaway: Take the square root before multiplying by the noise scale.

cards.title: What does 95% frequentist confidence mean?
cards.answer: Under repeated sampling, the interval-building procedure covers the fixed true parameter 95% of the time.
cards.takeaway: The coverage guarantee belongs to the procedure.

cards.title: Why is a new-response prediction interval wider than a mean-response interval?
cards.answer: A new response includes its own noise in addition to uncertainty in the estimated mean.
cards.takeaway: Predicting one noisy outcome is harder than estimating its average.

cards.title: With s=2 and mean-prediction leverage 0.25, what are the mean and new-response SEs?
cards.answer: Mean: 2√0.25=1. New response: 2√1.25=√5.
cards.takeaway: The extra 1 inside the square root is future observation noise.

cards.title: Do ten separate 95% intervals guarantee 95% coverage for all ten together?
cards.answer: No. All intervals covering simultaneously is a stronger event than any one covering.
cards.takeaway: More protected claims require more protection.

cards.title: What multiplier gives Scheffé protection for all coefficient combinations in a p-parameter Gaussian model?
cards.answer: √(pF), using the 1−α quantile of F with p and n−p degrees of freedom.
cards.takeaway: Protecting every linear combination widens the intervals.

cards.title: If A⊆B, which orthogonal complement is larger?
cards.answer: A⊥ is larger: B⊥⊆A⊥. Being perpendicular to a bigger space imposes more restrictions.
cards.takeaway: More directions to avoid means fewer directions left.

cards.title: Why is v₁+v₂ perpendicular to W₁∩W₂ when vᵢ is perpendicular to Wᵢ?
cards.answer: Any vector in the intersection is perpendicular to both v₁ and v₂, hence to their sum.
cards.takeaway: Two zero dot products still add to zero.

cards.title: In finite dimensions, what is (A⊥)⊥ for a subspace A?
cards.answer: A itself. Every vector decomposes into an A component and an A⊥ component; perpendicularity to A⊥ removes the latter.
cards.takeaway: Taking the orthogonal complement twice returns the original space.

cards.title: How does covariance change under AY+b?
cards.answer: It becomes AΣAᵀ. The constant shift b changes the mean, not the covariance.
cards.takeaway: Linear mixing changes spread; translation does not.

cards.title: Can X and X² be dependent but uncorrelated when X is standard normal?
cards.answer: Yes. Symmetry makes Cov(X,X²)=0, but X² is completely determined by X.
cards.takeaway: Zero correlation only rules out linear association.

cards.title: Can pairwise correlations miss multicollinearity?
cards.answer: Yes. One predictor can be nearly a combination of several others without nearly matching any single one.
cards.takeaway: Dependence can involve a group of columns.

cards.title: Why can nearly duplicate predictors have unstable coefficients but stable fits?
cards.answer: One coefficient can rise while the other falls, nearly cancelling in Xβ.
cards.takeaway: The data may identify a total much better than its parts.

cards.title: If predicting xⱼ from other predictors gives R²=0.95, what is its VIF?
cards.answer: 1/(1−0.95)=20. This is a variance-inflation factor under the usual regression comparison.
cards.takeaway: Little unique predictor variation means high coefficient uncertainty.

cards.title: If VIF=9, how much does the coefficient SE inflate?
cards.answer: By 3, holding noise and predictor scale fixed. Standard error is the square root of variance.
cards.takeaway: Variance factors must be square-rooted for SEs.

cards.title: Software reports GVIF^(1/(2df))=2. What is GVIF^(1/df)?
cards.answer: 4. Square the reported value.
cards.takeaway: Check whether a diagnostic uses a variance or SE-like scale.

cards.title: What does Gram–Schmidt subtract from the next column?
cards.answer: Its projection onto the earlier columns’ span. What remains is a new perpendicular direction.
cards.takeaway: Keep only what earlier directions cannot explain.

cards.title: Remove the projection onto (1,1) from (1,0). What remains?
cards.answer: (1/2,−1/2), whose dot product with (1,1) is zero.
cards.takeaway: Subtract the shared component to isolate a new direction.

cards.title: Does orthogonalizing predictors remove uncertainty in the original coefficients?
cards.answer: No. If all directions are retained, it only changes coordinates. Transforming back restores the original uncertainty.
cards.takeaway: A nicer basis is not new information.

cards.title: Why can PCR discard a useful predictor direction?
cards.answer: PCA ranks directions by variation in X, not their relationship with y. A low-variance direction may carry strong signal.
cards.takeaway: Large predictor variation need not mean high predictive value.

cards.title: Why does full-component PCR reproduce OLS, but truncated PCR may not?
cards.answer: All components preserve the original space. Dropping components removes directions from the model.
cards.takeaway: Rotation preserves a model; truncation changes it.

cards.title: Why fit PCA inside each cross-validation training fold?
cards.answer: Otherwise validation predictors influence the means, scales, and directions used to train the model.
cards.takeaway: Unsupervised preprocessing can still leak validation information.

cards.title: What does PLS use that PCA does not?
cards.answer: The response y, as well as predictor structure, to construct components.
cards.takeaway: PLS seeks response-related directions, not just variable predictors.

cards.title: Why is fitting PLS before splitting especially risky?
cards.answer: Validation responses influence the constructed components, leaking the answers into the representation.
cards.takeaway: Response-informed features must be trained without validation outcomes.

cards.title: Why does C(X) always contain zero?
cards.answer: Choose β=0, so Xβ=0.
cards.takeaway: A linear model space always passes through the origin.

cards.title: If Xβ₁ and Xβ₂ are possible means, is their sum possible too?
cards.answer: Yes: Xβ₁+Xβ₂=X(β₁+β₂).
cards.takeaway: Linear combinations stay in the model space.

cards.title: Does an OLS residual lie in N(X) or N(Xᵀ)?
cards.answer: N(Xᵀ), since Xᵀe=0. Residuals have n entries, not p.
cards.takeaway: Dimensions help catch a transposed-space mistake.

cards.title: A design has 10 rows and rank 3. How many residual directions remain?
cards.takeaway: Observation space splits into fitted and residual directions.
cards.source: Linear algebra notes · subspaces and rank · companion practice

cards.title: Can deleting a predictor enlarge the model’s column space?
cards.answer: No. Every combination of the remaining columns was already available.
cards.takeaway: Fewer ingredients cannot create more linear combinations.

cards.title: If X has full column rank, which coefficient contrasts are estimable?
cards.answer: Every ℓᵀβ. The row space is all of ℝᵖ.
cards.takeaway: No coefficient direction is invisible.

cards.title: How can a null vector prove that ℓᵀβ is not estimable?
cards.answer: Find v with Xv=0 but ℓᵀv≠0. Then β and β+v have identical means but different target values.
cards.takeaway: The data cannot distinguish targets that change invisibly.

cards.title: What does ℓᵀG(XᵀX)=ℓᵀ mean when G is a generalized inverse?
cards.answer: The target row survives the recoverable part of the design. This characterizes estimability in the notes.
cards.takeaway: Estimable targets live entirely in visible directions.

cards.title: Why do X and XᵀX have the same null space?
cards.answer: vᵀXᵀXv=‖Xv‖². This is zero exactly when Xv=0.
cards.takeaway: Squaring the design preserves its invisible directions.

cards.title: Why is C(XᵀX)=C(Xᵀ)?
cards.answer: They have the same null space, and their column spaces are the corresponding orthogonal complements.
cards.takeaway: The Gram matrix preserves the design’s visible coefficient space.

cards.title: For X=[x x], what is one nonzero null vector?
cards.answer: (1,−1). Increasing one coefficient and decreasing the other cancels exactly.
cards.takeaway: Opposing allocations leave the same total.

cards.title: With X=[x x], can the data identify β₁−β₂?
cards.answer: No. Shifting coefficients by (t,−t) changes the difference by 2t without changing the mean.
cards.takeaway: The unidentified direction is the contrast between duplicates.

cards.title: In μᵢⱼ=α+βᵢ+γⱼ, why isn’t α separately identifiable without constraints?
cards.answer: Add c to α and subtract c from every βᵢ. Every cell mean stays the same.
cards.takeaway: An arbitrary baseline can move between parameter blocks.

sources.locator: Least-squares theory · p. 2 · companion concept check

cards.title: In an observed additive two-way layout, is βᵢ−βₖ estimable?
cards.answer: Yes. At the same column j, μᵢⱼ−μₖⱼ=βᵢ−βₖ.
cards.takeaway: Compare groups while holding the other factor fixed.

sources.locator: Least-squares theory · p. 2 · companion concept check

cards.title: What does an additive two-way model assume about a row effect across columns?
cards.answer: The difference βᵢ−βₖ is the same at every column level.
cards.takeaway: Additivity means one factor does not modify the other’s effect.

sources.locator: Least-squares theory · p. 2 · companion concept check

cards.title: With all r×c cells observed, how many mean dimensions does an additive two-way model have?
cards.answer: r+c−1: one baseline, r−1 row contrasts, and c−1 column contrasts.
cards.takeaway: Redundant baselines should be counted only once.

cards.title: Why is “all group means are equal” different from choosing a reference group?
cards.answer: It removes allowable mean patterns. Choosing a reference only renames the same patterns.
cards.takeaway: A hypothesis changes the model; a coding convention need not.

cards.title: Can an invertible recoding change OLS residual SSE?
cards.answer: No. The fitted-value space and orthogonal projection are unchanged.
cards.takeaway: Different coefficients can produce identical fit quality.

sources.locator: HW2 · Q1 and Q4 · companion concept check

cards.title: Can individual coefficient p-values change after recoding?
cards.answer: Yes. A coefficient may now represent a different hypothesis, even though fitted values are unchanged.
cards.takeaway: Compare the tested contrasts, not just coefficient positions.

cards.title: When is the set β̂+N(X) a vector subspace?
cards.answer: When it contains zero, equivalently when Xβ̂=0.
cards.takeaway: A shifted space is linear only if the shift stays inside it.

cards.title: Why isn’t the line β₁+β₂=3 a vector space?
cards.answer: It excludes (0,0), and doubling a point changes the sum to 6.
cards.takeaway: Vector spaces must contain zero and survive scaling.

cards.title: What does Xᵀe=0 say about each predictor?
cards.answer: Its dot product with the residual is zero.
cards.takeaway: No available predictor direction remains in the residual.

cards.title: Why can least squares have no bad local minima?
cards.answer: Its Hessian is 2XᵀX, which is positive semidefinite because vᵀXᵀXv=‖Xv‖²≥0.
cards.takeaway: The squared-error surface is convex.

sources.locator: Least-squares theory · p. 9 · companion concept check

cards.title: When is the OLS coefficient minimum unique?
cards.answer: When X has full column rank, making XᵀX positive definite.
cards.takeaway: No flat coefficient direction means no alternate minimizer.

sources.locator: Least-squares theory · p. 9 · companion concept check

cards.title: Without an intercept, must OLS residuals average zero?
cards.answer: No. The all-ones direction may not belong to the model space.
cards.takeaway: Orthogonality only applies to directions the design includes.

sources.locator: Least-squares theory · p. 9 · companion concept check

cards.title: Why does ‖y‖²=‖ŷ‖²+‖e‖² for OLS?
cards.answer: Because y=ŷ+e and ŷᵀe=0.
cards.takeaway: The fitted and residual pieces form a right triangle.

cards.title: Why is I−P idempotent when P is?
cards.answer: Expand: (I−P)²=I−2P+P²=I−P.
cards.takeaway: Extracting the leftover twice changes nothing.

cards.title: Onto what space does the identity matrix project?
cards.answer: The entire observation space. Every vector stays unchanged.
cards.takeaway: Keeping every direction is also a projection.

cards.title: What does P=(1/n)11ᵀ do to y?
cards.answer: It replaces every entry with the sample mean.
cards.takeaway: The constant-vector space has one direction.

cards.title: Why does a projector’s trace equal its rank?
cards.answer: Its eigenvalues are only 0 and 1. Summing them counts the retained directions.
cards.takeaway: Trace counts the projector’s ones.

cards.title: If tr(H)=r for n observations, what is tr(I−H)?
cards.answer: n−r.
cards.takeaway: Every observation-space direction is fitted or residual.

cards.title: Can adding columns to an OLS model increase its minimized training SSE?
cards.answer: No. The old fit is still available in the larger space.
cards.takeaway: More options cannot worsen the best achievable training fit.

cards.title: What is rank(P₁−P₀) for nested spaces of dimensions r₀ and r₁?
cards.answer: r₁−r₀.
cards.takeaway: The difference projector keeps only newly added directions.

cards.title: What are the three orthogonal pieces in a nested-model decomposition?
cards.answer: Small-model fit, extra large-model fit, and large-model residual. Their sum is y.
cards.takeaway: Separate old signal, added fit, and leftover variation.

cards.title: Do arbitrary orthogonal projectors commute?
cards.answer: No. Nesting is one condition that makes P₀P₁=P₁P₀=P₀.
cards.takeaway: Do not move matrix factors past each other without a reason.

cards.title: Under sum coding, what does the intercept represent at zero numeric predictors?
cards.answer: The equally weighted average of fitted group means.
cards.takeaway: Zero-sum effects center the baseline across levels.

cards.title: Is a sum-coded intercept necessarily the overall sample mean?
cards.answer: No. It averages group means equally, while the sample mean weights groups by their sizes.
cards.takeaway: An average over groups differs from an average over observations.

cards.title: If you change the reference group, do group predictions change?
cards.answer: No, with equivalent full-rank coding and the same model. The differences are simply measured from a new baseline.
cards.takeaway: Changing the origin changes coordinates, not locations.

cards.title: Intercept 10 and effects 2,−1,−1 give which group means?
cards.answer: 12,9,9. Their equal-weight average is 10.
cards.takeaway: Add each deviation to the common baseline.

cards.title: A Helmert column has entries −1,−1,+2. How does its coefficient relate to C−average(A,B)?
cards.answer: That mean contrast equals three times the coefficient.
cards.takeaway: The contrast scaling sets the coefficient’s units.

cards.title: Why can the baseline-predictor slope stay unchanged across equivalent group codings?
cards.answer: The group-mean space is unchanged, so adjusting for it leaves the same regression problem for the numeric predictor, assuming identifiability.
cards.takeaway: Recoding a nuisance factor does not add or remove adjustment directions.

cards.title: What is the Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimate of σ² when SSE>0?
cards.answer: SSE/n, rather than SSE/(n−r).

cards.title: Why is SSE/n downward biased under the correct mean model?
cards.answer: Fitting removes noise along r model directions, leaving expected SSE=(n−r)σ².
cards.takeaway: The residual has already had some noise fitted away.

cards.answer: No. There are no residual degrees of freedom, and the denominator is zero.

cards.title: Does Gauss–Markov require normal errors?
cards.answer: No. The mean and spherical covariance assumptions are enough for the linear-unbiased comparison.
cards.takeaway: Normality is not part of BLUE’s core argument.

cards.title: Can a biased estimator have smaller mean squared error than BLUE?
cards.answer: Yes. BLUE only minimizes variance within the linear unbiased class.
cards.takeaway: Accepting some bias can reduce variance enough to help overall error.

cards.title: What does Var(y)=σ²I assert?
cards.answer: Equal marginal variances and zero pairwise covariances. It does not alone assert independence.
cards.takeaway: A covariance model is weaker than a full distribution model.

cards.title: When does the generalized-inverse condition force G=B⁻¹?
cards.answer: When B is invertible. Multiply BGB=B by B⁻¹ on both sides.
cards.takeaway: Full invertibility removes the freedom.

cards.title: How does the fitted-value projector act on C(X) and C(X)⊥?
cards.answer: It keeps the first and kills the second.
cards.takeaway: Those two actions completely determine the projection.

cards.title: If an alternative fit differs from the projection by length 3, how much extra squared error does it add?
cards.answer: 9, by the orthogonal squared-distance decomposition.
cards.takeaway: Distance within the model adds in quadrature.

cards.title: For full-rank X, when is By unbiased for β for every β?
cards.answer: When BX=I, because E[By]=BXβ.
cards.takeaway: Unbiasedness becomes a matrix identity.

cards.title: Why is AAᵀ positive semidefinite?
cards.answer: For every v, vᵀAAᵀv=‖Aᵀv‖²≥0.
cards.takeaway: A squared length can never reduce variance.

cards.title: Are GLS residuals necessarily Euclidean-orthogonal to X’s columns?
cards.answer: No. They satisfy XᵀV⁻¹e=0: weighted orthogonality.

cards.title: If Var(y)=σ²V, what covariance does V⁻¹ᐟ²y have?
cards.answer: σ²I.

cards.title: An average combines m independent equal-variance observations. What precision weight should it get?
cards.answer: Weight proportional to m, since its variance is σ²/m.
cards.takeaway: More independent measurements make an average more precise.

cards.title: Are inverse marginal variances alone enough for GLS with correlated errors?
cards.answer: No. The full inverse covariance matters, including off-diagonal entries.

cards.title: Why use the full model’s residual SSE in the F-test denominator?
cards.answer: It estimates noise after allowing all directions under consideration.
cards.takeaway: Use the leftover variation as the noise benchmark.

cards.title: Under the null, why is an F statistic often near 1 rather than 0?
cards.answer: Both numerator and denominator estimate the same noise variance after dividing by their degrees of freedom.
cards.takeaway: Added directions fit some noise even when no effect exists.

cards.title: Why can’t every coefficient restriction be tested in a rank-deficient model?
cards.answer: Some restrictions change along null directions while the data distribution stays the same.
cards.takeaway: A hypothesis must concern observable information.

cards.answer: XᵀXβ+Λᵀξ=Xᵀy, with multiplier scaling absorbed in ξ.

cards.title: Why use a t distribution instead of a standard normal when σ is estimated?
cards.answer: The estimated noise scale introduces extra uncertainty. Under Gaussian errors, the standardized coefficient uses t with n−p df.
cards.takeaway: Estimating the denominator makes the tails heavier.

cards.title: How do you build a pointwise coefficient confidence interval?
cards.answer: Estimate ± t critical value × estimated SE, under the Gaussian linear-model conditions.

cards.title: Does a frequentist 95% interval assign 95% posterior probability to its parameter range?
cards.answer: No. That interpretation needs a posterior distribution and its assumptions.
cards.takeaway: Coverage and posterior probability are different statements.

cards.title: Can unlimited data eliminate uncertainty in a new noisy response?
cards.answer: It can eliminate mean-estimation uncertainty in suitable settings, but not the new response’s irreducible noise.
cards.takeaway: Learning the average perfectly does not predict every outcome perfectly.

cards.title: Why might discarding small principal components help even though it loses information?
